utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Trial Chamber Rieneke Boterenbrood, who is a legal intern working with our team. She is from the Netherlands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue, there's a matter I would like to deal with. In assessing the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification which was filed on the 7th of November, 2013, and noting the Prosecution's response filed on the 18th of November, 2013, the Chamber notes that the accused has not provided sufficient details regarding the prior admission of five intercepts for which he requests that the Chamber take judicial notice of their authenticity. Therefore, as the Chamber has stated in the past, it instructs the accused, by 25th of November, 2013, to provide it with further information regarding the prior admission of the intercepts, including the transcript references or titles and date of the written decision through which they were admitted. Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to begin with something that you've alluded to during your examination-in-chief, and that was your trial and your conviction. Now, you were tried on charges related to and convicted for your participation as a member of a joint criminal enterprise along with persons such as Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic to forcibly remove Muslims and Croats from large areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including 35 municipalities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the way it was in the first judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And those municipalities included Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Bosanski Novi, Bratunac, Foca, Hadzici, Ilidza, Kljuc, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, Pale, Prijedor, Rogatica, Sanski Most, Sokolac, and Visegrad, Vlasenica, Vogosca, and Zvornik? Those were among the municipalities embraced by the indictment and the conviction; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the first indictment did contain these municipalities; however, in the first judgement some of them were dropped and in the second judgement many more were dropped. So what stayed on were the things that happened in nine municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the judgement is available for all to see. In fact, I'll be providing you with a copy of it in Serbian. I think you'll see that the conviction embraced more than nine municipalities, and we'll talk about some of those specific municipalities during the course of this examination. Now, in assessing your responsibility, the Trial Chamber found that your involvement was crucial to the commission of the crimes, and that's found at paragraph 1158 of your judgement. For your benefit, Mr. Krajisnik, I have a copy of the trial judgement in your language. This is 65 ter 24274, which has also been uploaded in both languages. And I'm referring to a finding that is reflected at paragraph 1158, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a lawyer, but as far as I understood this, the nine municipalities that remained in the conviction are Trnovo, Sokolac, Bratunac, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Prnjavor, Banja Luka, Sanski Most, and Krupa, and there's not a single event that occurred outside these municipalities that I was convicted for in the final judgement. I'm speaking to you as a former accused person, that is to say, a person who was convicted; but it is possible that from a legal point of view somebody may interpret this differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're welcome to turn to paragraph 1158, but I take it you will confirm that the Trial Chamber found that your involvement in these events was crucial to the commission of the crimes that were charged and for which you were convicted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first judgement and you are right. There were many municipalities in the first judgement. I, however, am speaking about the final judgement in which those municipalities were dropped. I'm telling you again how it is that I understand things. My participation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, excuse me. Let's -- okay. You were about to address your -- go ahead. Finish that thought. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then you shouldn't have interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I will feel free to interrupt you when you are not answering the question. In this case you started off on a different course, talking again about the municipalities, then you began to address the question I had raised. So you may continue if you're responsive to the question I've asked. Please continue, your participation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to give that kind of response because you made a mistake. You said I was convicted for 36 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please -- will you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was nine municipalities so I had to correct you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question is -- the question is: The Trial Chamber found that your involvement in the crimes was crucial to their commission? Yes or no? And I directed your attention to paragraph 1158. If you're unable to answer that question, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think that Mr. Tieger shouldn't adopt that kind of tone with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You referred to municipalities. It's fair enough for the witness to comment on that, but let's continue. Mr. Krajisnik, the -- please try to answer the question. Mr. Tieger's question about the passage in paragraph 1158 in your trial judgement in which your role was said to be crucial. Would you like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the judgement, the final judgement, my participation in the joint criminal enterprise was significant and I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Judges also included a special section that began at paragraph 888 on your credibility as a witness or your lack of credibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, you testified from April to June 2006, for 40 days or two and a half months on a four-day workweek. That was the length of your testimony before the Trial Chamber; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after watching you and hearing you for that period of time, the Trial Chamber found that you were a witness of "very low credibility." And that's found at paragraph 888 of your judgement; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are talking about the first-instance judgement. Please, that is not what the second-instance judgement says. Out of the 36 municipalities, I was convicted of nine, whereas in the other ones it was not confirmed, that is to say, what the trial judgement said. And that is what I had been saying all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you are well aware of the fact that you were convicted, whether you want to quibble about the number of municipalities or not, for your participation in a joint criminal enterprise, participation which you disputed for 40 days, for two and a half months of court, as a result of which the Trial Chamber found that you were a witness of very low credibility. And the Appeals Chamber didn't upset that finding in any way. They validated the position that your claims about your participation, your lack of participation in the JCE, were not true.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your statement that the first-instance Chamber said that my credibility was low is correct. I wish to explain to you that they also said what they said about the other 28 municipalities, that my testimony was correct; that's what the second-instance judgement said. And then that was proven to be wrong in terms of what the first-instance judgement had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will look at it and I'm not going to quibble, but you know very well -- and we were both there, Mr. Krajisnik, that your Defence is based on the fact that you were not involved in the JCE and you were ultimately convicted and the conviction was affirmed for your participation in the JCE. That's the bottom line. You said you didn't substantially contribute to a joint criminal enterprise and you were convicted for that and you served time for that. Are you unwilling to admit that to these Judges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I believe it would be useful for me to explain this because your approach is wrong. I told you, I am not denying that the first-instance judgement found me guilty, that my participation was significant. Also, I'm not denying that I was convicted as a member of a joint criminal enterprise for nine municipalities, for nine cases -- actually, several cases within those municipalities as a member of JCE. Also, I accept the judgement because it's a final judgement; however, I do not accept what happened. That is why I'm working on the review of that judgement. If you wish, every part of the judgement where I was found guilty, I'm going to prove here before this Chamber that your indictment was wrong and that the then-Trial Chamber had made a mistake. This, however, are not review proceedings, and that is why I believe it would be fair to know the entire truth so that a partial truth would not mislead the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to as much of the truth as we can. Let's just identify just a very few of the numerous areas where the Trial Chamber found that you were a witness of very low credibility. First of all, they found -- well, the Trial Chamber found numerous instances, in fact in excess of 20 as the judgement reflects. One of those, for example, is found at paragraph 890 of your judgement, where the Trial Chamber noted that you denied knowledge of many facts surrounding crimes committed by the Bosnian Serb authorities in 1992. And in 891 the Trial Chamber indicates that there was a large body of evidence directly proving your intent and knowledge. So that's one area and we'll address that more specifically during the course of this examination, but that's one thing that the Trial Chamber found; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the findings of the Trial Chamber, first-instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then paragraph 949 and 948 the Trial Chamber addressed in part your assertions regarding your relative powerlessness and found at paragraph 949 that, to the contrary, you had direct access to the levers of Bosnian Serb state power. Correct, that was the finding of the Trial Chamber? And I will be discussing with you during the examination here some aspects related to your role in the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is -- you confirm that that was another aspect of the Trial Chamber's findings with regard to your assertions and your credibility in connection with those?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for the Prosecutor not to torment himself, the Trial Chamber did find that my testimony was of low credibility. Full stop. So that is what is stated by all of these paragraphs and that is the first-instance judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. One more before I move on to a specific example, Mr. Krajisnik, that I think is illustrative. At paragraph 1037 of your judgement, 1036 and 1037, the Trial Chamber focused on your testimony concerning knowledge of the detention of civilians in 1992 and found that contrary to your testimony, that many of the facts about detention of civilians were known to you before August of 1992, that is, before the time that there was an international outcry following the entry of international journalists into Omarska. That's at paragraph 1037. So that's another aspect of what the Trial Chamber found, specific aspect of what the Trial Chamber found about your credibility concerning those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say to this day that this is wrong. And it is correct that that is what the Chamber stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, maybe it would be useful, rather than traversing through the many parts of the judgement that reflect the Trial Chamber's findings about your assertions and your credibility with respect to those, that we look to a particular example of your testimony in your previous case. And you may or may not recall this, Mr. Krajisnik, but I want to bring you back to your testimony in response to viewing the video of the rally that was held in Banja Luka on the 21st of August, 1994, a rally attended by you, Mr. Karadzic, and persons such as Mr. Radic, Mr. Kupresanin, and Mr. Brdjanin. Now --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the date of the rally?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: August 21st, 1994. I'm happy to show you that rally again if you need to see it and I'm happy to show you the transcript of what those persons said or a copy of -- or show you what was said in your trial about that. So you let me know if you need any of those things along the way. But at that rally, Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Brdjanin preceded you at the podium. And Mr. Kupresanin said: "There can be no Islamic state on land that has been forever Serbian. There is no Muslim people and the entire world knows this. There are only Serbian people in these parts." And that's at -- found at P00014, English pages 5 and B/C/S page 4. Then Mr. Brdjanin spoke, this is something that the Trial Chamber had an opportunity to see yesterday, saying: "Those leftist forces which are offering us coexistence again must know that it is the obligation of Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours." And then, Mr. Krajisnik, you spoke and you began by saying: "Dear brothers and sisters, having heard these wonderful words by my predecessors, I feel great satisfaction at being at this gathering here today." And that's found at P00014, English page 8 and B/C/S page 7, and it was discussed during your trial at transcript page 24946. Now, in response to that and upon being asked questions about your praising of these predecessors' remarks, you said that you were commenting only on Kupresanin's statement; that's found at 24949 of your trial transcript. You recall that was your position, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall; however, I can give you my comments right now as if I had never said anything before, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm interested in what you said to the Trial Chamber at the time, what you said the first time you were confronted with this. So I would like you to confirm or I'll show the transcript that you said despite the fact that you spoke about predecessors, plural, on August 1st, 1994, that you told the Trial Chamber, well, you were only commenting on Kupresanin's statement. That's the first thing. If you want to see the transcript and I'll read the transcript to you, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you that that's the way it was. There's no need for you to read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you said that you said those were wonderful statements only "in order to gloss over a statement I didn't agree with." So it was your testimony to the Trial Chamber that you didn't agree with Kupresanin's statement, but you said to the crowd: Those are -- that's a wonderful statement, in order to show your disagreement. That was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly the way it was, as I put it then. Today I do not agree with the negation of the Muslim nation because every person has the right to declare himself the way he feels. It is a very well-known thing that I do not agree with rhetoric that is not well-balanced. And it is wrong to say something like that especially at a big meeting like this one, a big rally like this one, things that were said by these other participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And you noted that Mr. Kupresanin denied the existence of the Muslims, everybody applauded, they applauded all kinds of nonsense. And you said you put your words in the way you did because you couldn't say: "Kupresanin, you're a criminal." So you -- that's correct, isn't it? And that's what you said to the Trial Chamber in your case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the translation is probably wrong. I would never have said that he was a criminal. I would prefer to say that he was wrong, that he was doing things in a rather unbalanced way. So this is probably a wrong interpretation. I don't agree with those Serbs who deny the right to the Muslims to have a nation, even though there are facts that prove that the Muslims descend from the Serbs, but if they don't want to be Serbs nowadays it's their wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, whether it was -- whether you considered it criminal or radical, as I believe you modified it to -- a little bit later in your testimony, the bottom line is that you were trying to explain to the Court that Kupresanin said something very, very wrong that you very much disagreed with. And you tried to explain your praise or your seeming praise of Kupresanin by calling it a wonderful statement by saying in fact you were very much against it. That was the position you took when you were first confronted with this video; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I said the same thing then. If a politician tries to deny something at a public rally, it has to be in a mild and moderate way and you start with the word "but" and then you get to the point. This rally took place during war time. It -- of course, it would be politically damaging to get into debates in such a rally. I say again, I don't think that this was criminal, what he said, that the Muslims were not the same as Serbs, but I thought that at the time that would be politically damaging and I disagreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, after you offered this explanation to your Trial Chamber about the motive for your comments and what you purported was your actual disagreement with Kupresanin, you were confronted with the fact that that wasn't the first time that Kupresanin had raised that point, that in fact he had raised that same point in the Assembly in January of 1993 and that not only did you not disagree with him, but you explicitly agreed with him, raised the issue on the agenda on the spot, backed it, and the result was a conclusion that Muslims were not a nation that was adopted at the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are misinterpreting this, Mr. Prosecutor, because you extracted a portion, just like last time, only one portion. It was not that I was right. I'm talking about Mr. Kupresanin. I made reference to Mr. Kupresanin's statement about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your answer and please speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters and us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll repeat. I'll try to repeat my answer. Mr. Prosecutor is wrong and I'm sorry to say that because he is entitled to criticise me, not I him. I would like Mr. Prosecutor to take a look at the comment that I made on Mr. Kupresanin's answer. It wasn't that I was right, but Mr. Kupresanin was right because my intention was to get involved in this raging debate to the effect that Kupresanin said that Muslims were not Serbs because on the day before at the Deputy Club, some deputies maintained the position that the whole people has the right to oppose the position of individuals. And the point is that a decision was to be made, although many deputies were against it, to the effect that the Muslims were not Serbs; however, that was not important, that was irrelevant. And for that reason I said: All right, I am wrong. You, Mr. Kupresanin, are right. The Muslims are not the Serbs. Let's move on. That doesn't mean that my opinion was that Mr. Kupresanin was right. If you look at the conclusions, you will not find it anywhere. Just for the rhetoric purposes, I told him: Mr. Kupresanin, I concede that you are right. Let's move on. That's the true meaning of my words. Mr. Prosecutor, please find the place where I said: I'm wrong and you, Mr. Kupresanin, are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, going back to the speech at the rally, in order to understand the real context in which Mr. Krajisnik said -- let me see, "wonderful words by my predecessors," probably the Chamber needs to read what followed that expression, i.e., the remaining parts of Mr. Krajisnik's speech on that day. But I note the -- they are redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, they weren't -- I originally offered the entirety of the video. I'm happy to do that now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- or the entirety of Mr. Krajisnik's remarks, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So probably the Chamber needs to read the remainder of Mr. Krajisnik's speech in order to understand what he meant at the time. Do you agree? Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that will be pages 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, I don't know until what part is Mr. Krajisnik's words, but I would like to -- the Chamber wants to see the remainder of Mr. Krajisnik's speech on that day. That said, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you say that the Prosecutor has a right to criticise you, but in fact you also assumed that right at the trial and also -- at your trial and also criticised Momcilo Krajisnik. So when you were -- when you heard and saw the words that you spoke on that date which belie what you're saying now, and let me just point out one portion of what you said, you said: "Let me explain why it isn't good. They want us to say we're all the same. They really want to create one nation, that we're all the same only of different religion. We must say that we are different" -- by the way this is found in pages 24966 and 67 of your transcript. "They are a group of Turkish orientation. Well, all right, people, if we accept that they are some kind of group, Turkish or I don't know who's, then we simply give them aces to their hands to be an independent nation. They will be more than happy to claim that they are of Turkish origin, the same as the Siptars developed theories that they are of Iliric origin. Why, we should tell them who they really are. They are unbelievers, a nation that is not a nation, that is to say a nation that would like to be a nation but has no arguments for a nation." And then you were asked whether or not your comments in response to Mr. Kupresanin's comments in 1994, that is, whether your earlier testimony at the rally was wrong because, in fact, in saying that you didn't disagree with Kupresanin and didn't deny the Muslims their right to be a nation, that was false because that's the position you took at the Assembly almost two years earlier. And you said at page 24967: "That's correct. This here is nonsense what Momcilo Krajisnik was saying. It's detrimental. I have to say I never thought like this. If I could distance myself from this Momcilo Krajisnik, I would." Do you remember that? Do you remember talking about the -- how embarrassed you were by what you called the -- that Momcilo Krajisnik and how what he was saying was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that comment of mine referred to one of my statements and that is that the Turks had occupied my village. Being enraged, I used the word "Turks," although it may not be derogatory but it might sound in this context. Without having any insight that this was occasioned by this event --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me put this in context for you. You did, in fact, offer the testimony that you never used the derogatory term "Turks." And then you were confronted -- that's right. And then you were confronted with at least one instance, I believe two, where it was obvious that you had done so, and that was another occasion on which you tried to distance yourself from that Momcilo Krajisnik, that other Momcilo Krajisnik, right, and that's what you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, only on one occasion did I distance myself from Momcilo Krajisnik and that was during the confrontation that you arranged when I said that I don't remember ever using the word "Turks." This is not a word in my vocabulary. Then, at the request of the Presiding Judge Orie, you put to me the fact that the Turks had occupied my village. It may also include the event of the 12th of May, and then I as I say that without you informing me that this is about this event, I said that I distanced myself from Momcilo Krajisnik. And I repeat it today to this Chamber, that there is no the word "Turks" in my vocabulary or any other derogatory word and everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina can confirm that, not that I'm different from other people, but simply because this is not fair. If you look at the entire context, you will find out that this was occasioned by the confrontation that was intended to confirm whether I ever used the word "Turks," and I used it only once when the Muslim army occupied the village and committed heinous crimes. And I said that when I was angered and that is why I used that word, but I don't remember speaking about this in the context of Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to quote from 24967 and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are going to quote, let us upload it. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last answer it was not recorded that witness said: Even though I said that in a situation when my village was occupied and the crimes had been committed, I'm not happy to have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Going back to the 1994 rally transcript, the Chamber may also need Kupresanin's part in its entirety as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I was told that we need also the video part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. We'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is short, then please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. It's 65 ter 25522, and we're talking about page 24967. And while we're waiting, I can also mention that the Assembly session that's been referenced is P921, the specific sections that were referenced were found at English pages 94 through 96 and B/C/S 64 through 66, but obviously the Court is -- has the entirety of the session in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Krajisnik, the question that you were asked was: "When you talked about your comments in response to Mr. Kupresanin's comments in 1994 by saying that you disagreed with him and you didn't deny the Muslims their right to be a nation, that was just wrong, wasn't it? "A. That's correct. This here is nonsense, what Momcilo Krajisnik was saying. It's detrimental. I have to say I never thought like this. If I could distance myself from this Momcilo Krajisnik, I would ..." If you look down toward the bottom of the page, you continue: "... this speech is absolutely authentic, and I'm very sorry that this Momcilo Krajisnik said what he said." And on the following page you said: "... I know what Kupresanin said but I spoke in a very indecent way because there is no reason why anybody should not be allowed to be a Muslim, a Croat, a Serb, whatever they please ..." So that was, indeed, another occasion on which you distanced yourself from that other Momcilo Krajisnik in response to being confronted with a contradiction between what you were saying in court and what you had said at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that this is a great surprise to me. I remember that I only commented this due to the event when the Muslim forces raided the village and occupied it. As for this comment, it's probably related to this, otherwise why would I distance myself from Momcilo Krajisnik and my speech? It turns out from here that I was supporting Mr. Kupresanin whilst I didn't. I don't know how this happened. I had no reason to say all of this because it wasn't me who used the word "Turks," it was Mr. Kupresanin. Therefore, I find it hard to understand, especially since it's in English, whether I am distancing myself from Mr. Kupresanin or from myself. I have no reason to distance from myself because I didn't say anything inappropriate and bad in my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, whether you now claim you had no reason to do so, Mr. Krajisnik, the transcript is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender those pages, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Tieger, the further parts of this page shows that Mr. -- Judge Orie offered Mr. Krajisnik to take the document with him to the Detention Unit so that he could have -- review the document and comment upon later on. So do you know what happened afterward?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President, and would be happy to tender those -- the entire -- what happened was Mr. Krajisnik took this position that he is essentially taking today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us ask the witness first whether he remembers what he did --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the result of his review of this document. Do you remember that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. I don't remember this sequence of events because I didn't have any reason to distance from myself in this particular instance. I could only have distanced myself from Mr. Kupresanin. However, in this first instance, I had a good reason for that which was prompted by the occupation of my village. There is obviously some kind of confusion here. I really don't understand why I would have distanced myself from the speech if I didn't say anything inappropriate in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to move on, but to resolve -- to satisfy the Court's inquiry, let me ask you if you're prepared to confirm this. You came back to court the next day and suggested that, having read this thing, that you were just repeating other people's words. And then the Trial Chamber looked to some of the previous words that were said, which included Mr. Corda saying: We also know that Muslims are not a nation. I would always stress that during the negotiations. They are degenerates. They are no ethnic community. They are our outcasts. That's at 24984. As it happened, you read out that passage to the Court but left out the degenerates quote. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are confusing me. You put three things to me at once. One is a speech in Banja Luka, and if we are talking about my apology regarding this speech, I didn't have any reason to apologise for my speech. The second event was the Assembly session, where a conclusion was adopted that Muslims were not a nation. And the third case was my distancing from Mr. Krajisnik when I called them Turks because they occupied my village. Now, I'm kindly asking you to refrain from this line of questioning because this will prove that I am not a reliable witness. Now, as for Mr. Corda and the Assembly session, I only repeated the words of various participants in the debate, both at the Deputies Club and in the Assembly session, just to allow them to reach this conclusion so that we could move on. And I didn't distance myself from myself but rather from the people who reacted in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we -- I've tendered those pages to the Court. I'm going to tender these pages as well. Just again to follow -- to assist the Court, then you continued to say that you were just trying to put it to a vote, that in any event the Assembly was not competent to make the determination of whether Muslims were a nation, and that you hadn't been the first to speak those words. And the Trial Chamber said the issue was not -- the issue was whether you spoke the words, not whether you were the first person in the Assembly to do so; and second, that no one had suggested that the Assembly was competent to do what it did. And the Trial Chamber said you are more or less engaging in a discussion with an unknown interlocutor; that's at 24988 through 89. Can you confirm that or is it preferable to actually allow the Trial Chamber to see exactly what you said in your trial after you had reviewed the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what I said in the trial and what my position was regarding the Assembly. If you remember, at the beginning Mr. Kupresanin's speech was presented, the one held in Banja Luka. Then my reaction followed prompted by the occupation of the village. Now, as for the Assembly, I still maintain that there was a lengthy discussion about this issue, both at the Deputies Club on the previous day and on the day itself, where people said many ugly things; and I reached a conclusion that this was all nonsensical. I said, without repeating their words, that what they did during this whole period produced a conclusion which was irrelevant. That's what I said then and I still say this, and this is what is recorded -- that -- and I remember that clearly. There were three things happening at the same time which probably created this confusion and it affected you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What pages are you tendering, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The pages that I previously identified, Mr. Chairman, and also 24983, where this discussion begins, to 24990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in this 65 ter document, 25522, I don't see transcript pages 24984 or 988 and 989. After page -- transcript page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thought the -- there are obviously multiple days of testimony and I don't know exactly how it was uploaded, but I thought it was all uploaded under the same 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After page -- transcript page 24980, which is e-court page 1903, follows the transcript page 24992, skipping some 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Must be an upload glitch. We'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I would like to look at it, but I don't think I'll have any -- if I can look at those and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you have no objection admitting the first two pages 24967 to 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit them and if you have objections, come back to the Chamber as soon as possible. We'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to turn to one more aspect of what the Trial Chamber found about -- in connection with its findings about your credibility. At paragraph 1005 of your judgement, the Trial Chamber examined part of your claims about your -- about the relationship between the leadership, the Bosnian Serb leadership, and the VRS and your claims that it was only logistical, had nothing to do with military operative issues, and found that this represented "another attempt by the Accused to mislead the Chamber into thinking that he was a weak and hierarchically isolated bureaucrat who dealt exclusively with inconsequential matters of administration, such as the supply of food and clothing." And the Trial Chamber found that this was "so incompatible with the evidence built up against him that it forced him down paths of obfuscation and incoherence." So that was another finding that the Trial Chamber made about your credibility in that instance related to your assertions concerning your relationship with the military and military operative matters; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to ask me a specific question and then the Chamber would see that. There is no reason for you to repeat the wording of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was a long trial, Mr. Krajisnik, as I have just indicated. I'm asking you about the Trial Chamber's findings, findings which your statement here to this Court -- your testimony to this Court purports to dispute. So I'm asking you to confirm at the outset that that is what the Trial Chamber found or I can tender that portion of the judgement if you dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what did I deny here before this Trial Chamber which is contained here? I don't -- I'm not aware of anything that I denied or refuted. Perhaps it's a misunderstanding and perhaps you are concluding something that I don't understand. I did not deny anything that is written in the judgement here. Whatever you have read, I said it's correct. So I don't see what it is that I am denying what is included here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look specifically at some of the things you testified to previously as well as some of the things you said to this Court in your testimony earlier. First of all, in your own case in 2006 you said specifically at transcript page 25619 that at the meetings with the military, they just thought of the civilian authorities as logistical support and "no discussion of military operative issues." So that was the position you took in 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still claim today that the maximum percentage, let me say practically all the questions, the issues requested by the army was to support them logistically. All the information that we received then were general and there was not a single -- or there were just some indications but no information about crimes reached us. That was why I explained then and I'm saying now. The army came and always raised the issues about the logistics so that it would be provided so that it could wage the war, and that was the purpose of the civilian authorities. The information that we received at those meetings were general. Except for some pieces of circumstantial evidence and criticism against the civilian authorities, I never heard anything about things that I learned later at this Tribunal. So this is the truthful and correct answer and this is what I said then as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned some meetings. You also mentioned meetings back in 2006, in particular a few meetings with General Mladic. You said at 25619 that you didn't attend many meetings, correct, that is with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether General Mladic was with somebody else, but everything that I learned from these materials, the meetings of the Presidency, where it stated that General Mladic attended them, that's correct. There were two or three briefings, that's also correct. Probably there was a series of meetings that he attended but that I didn't attend, but I haven't been informed about them here. If you mention specifically a meeting, I will tell you whether I attended it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you just generally seemed to indicate, you said with respect to those not many meetings with General Mladic that you attended, you mentioned two Presidency sessions; that reference is found at 25736. And you also mentioned two consultations with the military, one at Bijeljina, one at Pale; and that reference is found at 25684. So those were four meetings that you -- meetings at which General Mladic was present that you referenced when you said you didn't attend many meetings with General Mladic. Is that your position here before this Court today, that that is roughly the number of meetings that you had at which General Mladic was also in attendance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it wasn't only that meeting. There was one with Mr. Carter and once I was in Crna Rijeka when Mladic was there. But the meetings that you mentioned now were a subject of discussion here. I said that I attended them. If you mention a different, another meeting, which I did not mention, I will tell you no, I didn't because nobody asked me about it. Your question is not clear to me. You probably mean that other leaders were together with Mladic and not myself, which is also true. Mr. Koljevic as the president of the committee that was in charge of co-operation with UNPROFOR, Ms. Plavsic as well, there were individual meetings that I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. No, I was only trying to find out if your reference to not many meetings and then your specific identification of two Presidency meetings and two consultations generally reflected the limited number of meetings that you had with General Mladic or, if following your testimony, you suddenly recall dozens more.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, Mr. Prosecutor. I said then that there were few meetings that General Mladic had with the leadership that I attended and that's correct. Those meetings which were christened as the meetings of the expanded Presidency, I said that that's correct and that I did attend them. And other individual meetings that he had with some individual leaders or some other meetings that perhaps he may have attended, I did not attend them. I may have attended a meeting that is not recorded here, but we never discussed that, nor did anyone ever ask me: Did you attend this meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, you also explained that you knew little to nothing about military matters. For example, you said you did not know what goals were being implemented by the military; that's at 25595. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was waging the war. How was it doing it? What were the specific tasks? I didn't know that. Whether they needed to take a place or not, that was the competence of the army. I knew that the army had two or three tasks: To protect the Serbian people, not to allow a genocide to be perpetrated like in Second World War, and to stay militarily on the ethnic lines which armed people had taken in the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked whether you recall ever asking at any of these few meetings you say you attended what goals were being pursued by the military, and you -- your answer was at page 25619: "I can't remember what I did. I don't remember having asked such a question." And that's also what you testified to in 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember whether that question was asked, whether I said so in 2006, as it was quite a long time ago. But if that's in the record, then it must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can either tender that or I guess we can address --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if you want me to deal with these sequentially, Mr. President. That sounds like one where we would normally actually tender the quote so you could see it. But let me just put that on the record and we can resolve that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add these pages. But could you be more specific about the pages you're tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. It was 25619 and 25595.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know about intentions to issue directives and didn't ask because it wasn't your "interest or competence." Correct? Now I'm talking about directives, military directives.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an outsider I could become interested about the specific case, but it wasn't within my purview. I didn't know when the directives were signed or how they had been drawn up. It was simply the competence of other people. I could inquire accidentally, but in principle I certainly didn't deal with this nor was that within my purview or within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, when Judge Hanoteau asked you specifically whether you took advantage of the presence of those military figures to ask what was going on, you said: "As for their intentions to issue directives, I never asked about that because it wasn't my province." That's at 25703 through 04.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we need to be clearer. Let me repeat, I wasn't informed about when they did it. I didn't inquire nor was that my competence. I may have asked accidentally, I do not rule that out, but it was like having an outsider coming and inquiring or just attending a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what asking accidentally means, Mr. Krajisnik. But I note that you said in 2006 that you never asked about that because it wasn't your province. That's a correct reflection of what you stated to the Court in 2006, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be precise. That's why I say it certainly wasn't my competence. I didn't inquire about that. I'm saying now I may have asked somebody something accidentally if I happened to attend a meeting, but it was as if you had been present at the meeting rather than myself. It wasn't anything so important. My attendance, my presence, was not so important that anyone would brief me or report to me about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's similar to what you said in 2006, the latter part anyway, you were asked whether the military kept the political authorities apprised of operations that were about to be or that were conducted, and you said: "I don't remember that anybody informed me of actions like this before they happened. Whether they copied such documents to somebody else, I don't know." That's at transcript 25608 through 09. That's what you said in 2006, right, in response to that inquiry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that the Main Staff had no need or obligation to send information to me. It's possible that some information or report was sent to me, but everything that I read, even later on, was a sort of information as when a TV presenter reads something in the news, no crimes or anything that would be alarming or important, especially not for this Tribunal. That was why I said that I don't remember I was informed. I'm convinced that they did not inform me about anything, but I cannot rule out that perhaps some information may have reached me at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want us to get confused. I understand what you -- that you have taken the position that you never received any information about crimes whatsoever, but you did understand that my question referred not to being briefed about crimes but to being told about military operations before they would happen or after they had taken place. That's the question that was put to you in 2006 and that I asked you to either confirm or dispute. So were you answering a question about operations generally or limiting yourself to information about crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Receiving information from the Main Staff may have happened only exceptionally, that someone would inform me about something. In regularly informing me, as they were obliged to inform somebody else, I'm telling you that that was not usual way that the Main Staff was organised or had an obligation to do it. If there are any examples, those are individual examples and the contents were benign, without any particular importance. Some things I learned more from the TV than from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's your position that if you happened to be informed about a military operation before it was to be conducted or that after it had happened or while it was happening, that was only inconsequential or accidental?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm telling you before this Trial Chamber, the army was organised in such a way that they were not obliged to inform the Assembly or myself about the beginning of operations or the end of operations. It's possible that there were some instances when information did reach me, but that was not something that the Main Staff had to do, as far as I remember. And if you give me a specific example, I will comment on that. There was no single information, let me not say not a single piece of information, but information generally did not reach me that would describe that they would take certain territory, expel someone, or anything that would be considered as consequential and that I should comment on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to probably tender this, but just to -- one final thing. Mr. Krajisnik, I am not asking you whether there was a de jure responsibility on the part -- whether you consider that there was a de jure responsibility on the part of the VRS to inform you. I'm asking you about whether, as you were asked in 2006, the political authorities were apprised of operations that were about to be or were conducted. And I was simply confronting you with your testimony at that time, that you didn't remember that anybody informed you of actions like that before they happened, but you didn't know whether they copied such documents to somebody else. So your recollection in 2006 was that you weren't informed about actions -- military operations before they happened or after they took place; right? Whether there was a response -- a de jure responsibility to do so one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I then said that and I confirm it today. I only add it's possible that there may have been some individual reports, but I could not remember it then and I cannot remember it now, unless you present such reports to me and then I may have -- I may be able to tell you why I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in fact, in light of your assertions during your testimony in your own trial that you didn't have knowledge about military matters, you repeatedly suggested to the Trial Chamber that if it wanted to know about such matters, they should ask Mr. Karadzic. So, for example, when you were asked about an excerpt from a combat-readiness report - in this case that's admitted as D325 and the particular reference is found at page 159 in the English, B/C/S 138 - an excerpt that says explicitly that the army carried out the objectives put to it by the political leadership, you said that you didn't issue any orders and: "I don't know anything about that communication. Mr. Karadzic knows that." That's at transcript page 21669. That's what you said in your trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic had a military office and it's possible that he got --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik, first --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- such information. That's why I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First things first. Did you say that? And then you can offer the added information you want. That's what you said in your trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is written in the transcript and if it was not objected to, then that's the way it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I do not recall those words exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies. That's what you said when you testified in the Popovic case, in fact. I don't know if that helps refresh your recollection that you said that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think to this day, but I don't know if I said that then. I think that to this day. That was not my line of work and no one was supposed to inform me about that. That's what I think to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, in the Popovic case, you were asked about another section of the combat-readiness report, and we can -- the Popovic case transcript is 65 ter 25523. And you were asked about a section of the combat-readiness report that says that the strategic objectives of the war were promptly set and served as guide-lines and the Main Staff translated them into operational and tactical formations, et cetera. And then asked: So didn't the army strive to achieve the objectives put before it by the political leadership? And you answered: "Well," this is found at 21668, "well, I was not a supreme commander. I did not write support," that's how it's written, "I cannot help you. And you said to ask Gvero or other generals or "Mr. Karadzic when you bring him here." So again, in the Popovic case when asked about the goals put to the army and about operational military issues, you suggested to the Trial Chamber that they ask Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want to make me and Karadzic quarrel. Obviously that's your intention. You are misinterpreting something. I wasn't speaking about Mr. Karadzic as someone who was guilty of that. Mr. Karadzic was the supreme commander, and he is best-placed to interpret a directive if he signed it and if somebody reported to him. That is what I'm saying today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I tender those two excerpts, Mr. President, from 25523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two excerpts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President. Also, Mr. President, I've had a chance to look at my own copy of those pages, 24983 to 24990, of Mr. Krajisnik's trial, and I don't have any objection to those being added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time. Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For half an hour and resume at 11.00. Just a second. We'll assign a number for the Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 25523 will be Exhibit P6517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Svetlana Atanasova from Bulgaria who's joining us and she's a legal intern with our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just so there's no mistake. I'm not sure if -- we tendered two pages from 25523. The transcript gives the impression that the entirety of the document was tendered and admitted. I presume that's the relevant pages, but I just note that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, continuing on the subject of your knowledge of military operations, Mr. Krajisnik, despite your assertions that you knew very little about the planning or realisation of military operations, you nevertheless claimed that there was no planning for military operations. For example, as you said here to this Trial Chamber, at transcript page 44302: "Every ethnic unit took up its ethnic borders with slight corrections. The army only corrected some things or lost some territories or gave a different physiog nomy to that map." It didn't conquer those territories. And as you said in your testimony in 2006 at transcript page 25705 with respect to directives, all of them were issued and none were carried out. It all depended on developments in the field. There was not much planning in advance. It would just happen that you would lose a territory or gain a territory. There was no plan. So the latter quote is an accurate reflection of what you told the Trial Chamber in your own case in 2006, right, that there wasn't much planning in advance, it just kind of happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the military did do some planning, but the civilian leadership taking part in planning some operations, I do not recall any such plans and I can stand by what I said then as far as the civilian authorities are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I just want you to confirm or dispute that what you said in 2006 that with respect to developments in the field, that is what happened on the ground with the military, that: "There was not much planning in advance. It would just happen that you would lose a territory or gain a territory. There was no plan." That's at 25705. So you were saying in addition to the fact as you just mentioned here, that as far as you're concerned it had nothing -- military operations had nothing to do with the civilian authorities, that you also took the position that you were unaware of any -- not that you were unaware, that you took the position that there really wasn't any particular military operation plan, events just happened according to developments in the field?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that your question -- or perhaps the interpretation is not good. I'm going to repeat what it was that I thought then and what it is that I think today. Most of the territory of Republika Srpska was liberated, as the Serbs put it because this was their ethnic area, during the first time when the war started. After the army was established, later on there were a few major operations but, for the most part, that was the volume that stayed on with some minor corrections, perhaps. So my answer then was with a view to the following: All the ethnic communities stood at the beginning of the war at their natural ethnic boundaries and throughout the war, with some minor oscillations, they did not change all the way up until the end of the war, when we lost a lot of our territories and when the Muslim side lost some and the Croat side lost some, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 25705, Mr. President -- or page 25705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will add that. It's from the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is from the Krajisnik trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Krajisnik trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also said in response -- in your own trial in response to a comment by the Presiding Judge that it sounded as if you were saying you had no idea of where the army would end up, whether it was somewhere in Bosnia or in Italy, and you said: "The soldiers had only one goal, to hold the front line, and if they took any action in certain areas it would depend on the situation." And you said: "This was the only goal I was aware of." And that's at 25619 through 25620. Is that a correct -- again, you can see the transcript pages, but can you confirm or do you dispute that that's what you said to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber during the course of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that to the Trial Chamber, but just a small addition is required. All three parties, all three sides, if I can put it that way, there were armed people on all three sides and everybody was defending their own ethnic areas where they lived or at first somebody would take a bit more than they were entitled to, but these were minor corrections. The task and the wish of the local population was to always take part of the territory of the other side because in every part of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were the fellow countrymen of the people who had those wishes. So it was not a wish to extend territory because everyone felt that they had this right, to join their fellow countrymen who stayed on the other side to their own territory. On the other hand, the Serb army that constituted the armed people was to preserve the front because all of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a front line. That is the longest part in Bosnia-Herzegovina between two parties, between three parties, there was a front line. So that what I said stands and I add this to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition, despite your claims about limited knowledge about military operation, you insisted during your testimony in the Krajisnik case - and as you did here - that the strategic objectives annunciated at the 16th Assembly Session on May 12th by Dr. Karadzic were not military tasks of the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely asserted that and I assert that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you claimed that the strategic objectives were essentially putting down on paper what had been said to or proposed to Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but there is just this one small addition. The Neretva valley was placed within our strategic objectives on the basis of the talks held between the Serb delegation and the Croat delegation in Graz. As for the rest, all of it is actually copied parts of the map that we gave to Mr. Cutileiro before the Cutileiro Plan. As for the corridor, let me just say that too, that was also the subject of talks with the Croat side in Graz. I think it was on the 7th of May, if I remember correctly, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you say that -- you said in the Krajisnik case that the strategic goals were simply putting down on paper what had been put to Cutileiro, but now you're explaining that strategic objective number 4 or at least part of strategic objective number 4 related to the Neretva was not part of the Cutileiro proposal. So the strategic objective number 4 was not part of the Cutileiro Plan or proposal, that's number one; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the strategic objectives were actually our requests that were put to Mr. Cutileiro. We said to Mr. Cutileiro that we wished to have contiguous territory as far as the corridor is concerned. We said that we needed the Neretva River Valley; however, our strategic objectives followed after the talks held with the Croat side. As for these two objectives, a preliminary agreement had been reached specifically about the exchange of territories, about us giving concessions at critical points where the Croats needed something and vice versa. So there was the Cutileiro Plan, but we also reinforced and spelled out in concrete terms our own requests with a lot more certainty after the talks we had with the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So those were -- that's with respect to strategic objective number 4, that's the Neretva, and strategic objective number 2, the Posavina corridor; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also explained in your testimony in the Krajisnik case that strategic goal number 6, access to the sea, was something else that the Cutileiro Plan didn't embrace? That's at transcript page 24200.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Access to the sea was present in all our talks with Mr. Cutileiro, the representatives of the international community, later on the Croat side, and later on at conferences. Our request was for Bosnia-Herzegovina to have access to the sea and if Bosnia and Herzegovina were to be transformed into three ethnic entities, that we should have access to the sea there. There were combinations later on as well, to the effect that our right in the area of Neum would be replaced through exchanges of territory in the area of Molunat and Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear on this, this discussion about exchanges of territory, that took place in bilateral discussions with the Croats, right, between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all conferences, later on too, of course, under the auspices of the international community a proposal was worked out as to how this exchange of territories would take place and this partial agreement was reached in Dayton too. However, the participants in the talks forgot, if I can put it that way, to insert that and that did exist. There's also a map and also there is a written document as to how this would be carried out. It was never a secret that there would be a triple exchange of territories and it was never a secret that the Serbs should get access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two things. First of all, you explained repeatedly in your Krajisnik testimony or you asserted in your Krajisnik testimony that the exchange of territories that were contemplated was something that "we agreed on in Graz," and the Graz -- that's at 25598. So you explained that there was going to be -- that there was anticipated the possibility of obtaining the corridor by an exchange of territories and that's what was agreed on in Graz. First of all, that's what you said in your Krajisnik testimony at 25598; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because the Cutileiro Plan allowed for that; namely, that the parties, the negotiating parties, had the right to agree on territorial changes. As for the corridor, we were supposed to give part of the territory around Kupres so that the Croat parts of territory that would be part of the corridor would become Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Graz was a discussion between -- primarily between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban, but whatever other representatives of the Serbs and Croats participated, it was a discussion between the Serbs and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Graz there were two delegations that participated in the talks. After returning from a session or conference, when this conference did not end successfully, and then Mr. Cutileiro's proposal was: Try to resolve problems through bilateral agreements and talks. We availed ourselves of that opportunity, and then when we returned to Sarajevo -- so it was not only Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban, but there were two delegations that met and discussed all these questions, including this exchange of territories, Serb for Croat, Croat for Serb, and that was based on an agreement that had been reached beforehand in the Cutileiro map. These were territories that unequivocally belonged either to the Serb or the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Cutileiro map, that's the map that you presented, a coloured map, with the Cyrillic writing that you presented to this Court during the course of your examination-in-chief by Mr. Karadzic, right? That's what you're calling the Cutileiro map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a document here -- actually, it's a photocopy of the "Politika" daily newspaper of the 18th of March or the 17th. The Defence can find it. That map is the Cutileiro map that I talked about last time. It's in colour, as you said, and that is how you are going to see exactly those parts of territory that we were supposed to exchange on the basis of those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You -- we'll come to the Cutileiro discussions and the Cutileiro map, Mr. Krajisnik. I'll stay on the subject of military operations. You also explained during your Krajisnik testimony what you asserted to be the meaning of the strategic objectives. So, for example, you explained that strategic objective number 3 was -- which referred to the Drina, was in fact the elimination of a "psychological border through soft border controls." And that's found at transcript page 24158 and 24159. Is that right? "Our goal was for the psychological border on the Drina not to be there for the Serbs ..." And then -- that's at 24158. And then you discussed the "soft border" at 24159. Something that would be easy to cross, where you wouldn't need a visa, that's also at 24158. That's what you claim strategic objective number 3 was; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I claimed and that's what I claim now, and then I invoked Mr. Izetbegovic's book, his memoir, that is literally what he wrote in his book, that the Serbs should not feel that they were confined within boundaries, that there shouldn't be any passports and so on. You will be able to find that easily in the evidence that I provided during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you participated in the formulation of the strategic objectives, correct, and that's what you told the Krajisnik Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I even said that I think that I made this proposal or Mr. Karadzic, I don't know exactly which one of us, at this preparatory meeting. It was either Mr. Karadzic or I that formulated that or several of us, but at any rate I did take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were confronted during the course of your testimony with General Mladic's comments at the 16th Assembly Session, where he said he also participated in the formulation of the strategic objectives. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so but I don't know. I don't remember that quotation, but I do not rule out the possibility that that was said and that he was present when the strategic objectives were being formulated. I don't exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, he didn't -- it's not a question of his presence. I mean, first of all, let's be clear on this. What you said in your Krajisnik case is -- and you just affirmed right now, you think it was you who had the idea: Gee, let's put down what we're saying to Cutileiro, let's put it into some kind of exposition so that people will know about it. And then the people who were presumably participating in the Cutileiro discussions assisted in drafting the document; right? That's your testimony, and it was your testimony for the Krajisnik case as well at 24123 through 24125.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain that it was I who drafted it, but I leave it open that it possibly could have been Mr. Karadzic and myself. But it is true that I took part in the drafting of the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And so then General Mladic stood up at the 16th and said that he -- he talked about setting goals that can be achieved. He said: "I said this in Nevesinje before the top leadership of Republika Srpska and before an even more select political leadership in Belgrade." That's at P5956 at English page 35 and B/C/S page 26. And it was raised with you at transcript page 25531. And then he said at page 36 in the English, page 27 in the B/C/S: "It was discussed in the most select circle of comrades whom we convened the strategic goals that are of substance, which does not mean that they could not be better, richer or more in keeping with our current strength in the present moment." So that -- that seems to be a reflection of General Mladic saying that he participated in their formulation and in the discussion about their formulation and how they should be said and what kind of goals were appropriate. He wasn't a Cutileiro discussion expert like you, was he, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic did not participate in the discussions with Mr. Cutileiro. I'm almost certain that Mr. Mladic hadn't taken part in formulating the strategic goals. What we used to call at the time the Council for National Security was the body that discussed these issues, and it was at this body that the strategic goals were drafted. Now, as for the reference to Nevesinje, immediately before that it was recorded that Mr. Mladic and Mr. Ostojic had visited Nevesinje. Although we were not together, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic, and I also visited Nevesinje, but we did not meet with them. We did not discuss any strategic goals with the people from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in light of the fact that the strategic objectives, according to you, were strictly political, there would have been no reason for General Mladic, as he said at the 16th Session, to participate in their formulation, and particularly no reason if he knew nothing about the Cutileiro discussions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before going to the session, he could have familiarised himself with that. It was not a secret. We took this list of objectives to the session to present it to the MPs, that was to be done by Mr. Karadzic, and he was to explain what our position in the negotiations was and what we advocated in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. But according to you, that had nothing to do with General Mladic; that was strictly political and his job was military, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that it wasn't Mr. Mladic who formulated the goals. It was done either by Karadzic or Krajisnik, and it was adopted by the people who were present there. I do not rule out the possibility that at one of the preparatory meetings Mladic was there in order to familiarise himself with that, but it is highly unlikely because he was not a commander at the time, he was a member of the military. He could have been informed about that at some other meeting. He did not take part in formulating the objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, during the course of your testimony in your own case you were asked which members of the political leadership met with General Mladic before the 12th -- before the 16th Session and before his formal ascension to the top position of the VRS. And your answer was: "I don't know. I don't remember that I met with him and I didn't speak with him about any strategy or any goals if I did meet with him." That's 25531 through 25532. That's what you said during your testimony to the Krajisnik Trial Chamber, Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen several documents to the effect that there was some meeting, but to this date I don't remember that meeting and I would give the same answer today as the one that I gave at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And your answer was: You don't remember such a meeting, that's what you're saying now. But if you did meet with him, you didn't speak with him about any strategy or any goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I reiterate, it is possible that the strategic goals were drafted as such, that somebody informed Mr. Mladic about them, but the very drafting of the goals did not imply that we should discuss them. Rather, we wanted to inform the parliament about our position in the negotiations.
