And we definitely did not discuss the goals with him because he became the military commander only later; at the time he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I tender those pages, Mr. President, 25531 through 25532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic asked you about a Milovanovic quote in an interview - that's at transcript page 43302 through 03 - in which Mr. Milovanovic was quoted as saying something to the effect that the objectives of the war were to protect the Serbian people from destruction and to stay within Yugoslavia or, alternatively, have their own state. Now, those are fairly broad and I think you would agree those are not exactly the articulation of a specific military objective; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact strategic goals quoted by Mr. Milovanovic are in the directive. They are different from these ones. They're only given the same name. However, this confirms what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a quick look at D2149. This is a document tendered by Mr. Karadzic to this Trial Chamber and it's excerpts from General Milovanovic's notes on meetings with Karadzic. And this is English page 27, B/C/S 18 through 19. This particular note begins that: "On 25 July, the Main Staff ordered me to brief the Supreme Command on the results of a recently completed second phase of our offensive, Lukavac 93. Briefing of the Supreme Command took place." And then it continues: "With this I said the VRS had completed five of the six strategic war objectives and getting RS access to the sea was the only one remaining but could not be achieved by military means. Instead, this should be done using political and legal means." In contrast to the broad formulations that were quoted to you by Mr. Karadzic during your examination-in-chief, this reflects General Milovanovic's contemporaneous understanding of the military role in the implementation and attainment of the six strategic objectives, including access to the sea, which is strategic objective number 6, which was difficult to obtain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Milovanovic's understanding was. You have to ask him that. All I can say that the strategic goals formulated on the 12th of May were the platform translated into other form of what we discussed with Mr. Cutileiro. The access to the sea was a goal that was most easily achievable by military means, and the army could have done that because the JNA that was deployed at Prevlaka could just give this space and be replaced by the Army of Republika Srpska. But obviously that wasn't their goal because they preferred a political solution rather than a military one, and you can glean that from the documents that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation of the document is wrong. There are a few mistakes on this page alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, there's a -- I would like you to deal with separately if it relates to the document we have admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document, if I may add, we admitted, that tendered by the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We also saw in that excerpt General Milovanovic talking about the completion of those objectives to a large extent, as he put it there. In fact, the army was actively engaged, that's the VRS, in creating a factual situation that would improve the ultimate negotiations that would resolve -- ultimately resolve the conflict; right? And the factual -- well, just answer that first.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the logic behind it, but according to this logic there is sharp contrast. Since 18th of June, when Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic were in London, they signed a declaration with the then-foreign minister, Mr. Hurd, in which it was stated that the Serbian side undertook an obligation that should a peaceful solution be reached to return certain territories. Therefore, why should have been any taking of the territory that would then have to be returned to a much larger extent? Always, we wanted to achieve what we wanted to achieve with regard to territories at the negotiating table rather than on a battle-field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Date of this briefing, year is 1993, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Krajisnik, that the Bosnian Serb leadership never asserted that the new reality created by the demographic changes should be the basis for the -- at least part of the settlement and that Serbs claimed certain territories on the basis of a so-called right that came out of that new reality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one opinion. There were a variety of publicly expressed opinions. Everybody wanted to be a general or a politician. Even politicians used this kind of rhetoric in order to appease or to alleviate certain tones. I'm telling you what our policy was and what was laid down in the documents as our obligation and what was eventually achieved. We had always been prepared to cede a large chunk of the territory just to reach a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were too fast. Could you repeat from where you said: "We had always been prepared to cede a large chunk of the territory ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for speaking fast. Mr. Tieger, an old acquaintance of mine, inspires me to speak fast. At all times the Serbian policies and politicians were ready to cede a part of territory in order to achieve a peaceful solution. This policy was contained in a series of official documents. One of those documents was in a map in Mr. Owen's book that I presented to this Chamber, where 30 per cent of the territory that was either liberated or occupied by the Serbian army that we were prepared to return. Therefore, it is illogical for our army to go and conquer new territory so that we must return more. The year of 1993 was the year when our army was most successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've seen examples of -- you spoke about everybody having an opinion, everybody wanted to be a general or a politician. We've seen examples of Dr. Karadzic saying that he said to the international community when asked: Who gives you a right to Zvornik, which of course had been the majority Muslim municipality before the conflict, we said, according to him: "The right which comes out of a new reality," that's at the 46th Session, "explain if you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you need a new war to expel the Serbs back to Zenica. "We requested Zvornik according to this right." That was addressed to you in your own trial at transcript page 24932. You know that Dr. Karadzic said it. You know from your participation in the 46th Assembly. You know from talking about it at your own trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was mentioned at my trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic wasn't the only one who talked about the factual situation and the impact of the military results. General Mladic -- General Mladic said at the 34th Assembly Session that, first, the people and the army have carried out most of the tasks and strategic goals set to them. And then further: "You have started from the most favourable position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands. You and the people and the army and the forces of the MUP have created it." So General Mladic took the position that the VRS established, through its military operations, the most favourable position which could be exploited in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a big difference between what Mr. Mladic said and what Mr. Karadzic said. Mr. Karadzic wanted to appease the Serbs who, according to the maps, remained within the Federation. For example, in Zenica and other areas as well as the central parts of Sarajevo. There were many more Serbs there than in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said: This is the factual situation. At this moment we cannot give Zvornik to the Muslims because, quite simply, the Serbs will not return, they will be refugees, and that would be unjust. As for Mr. Mladic, you cannot expect a general who is a professional soldier who wages war, it is only to be expected that his achievements and the job that he is assigned to is something that he was going to praise and magnify. And the tradition is whatever you occupy you can keep. But look at other excerpts from Mr. Karadzic's speeches. We are ready to return some of the territories and we are ready for a peaceful solution. And I say that there is a big difference between the two. The one is speaking as a soldier, who is enhancing the importance of his job, whereas the other is speaking as a politician who realises that some people, according to the maps, had been left in the Federation. This is what we discussed with people, with the international community, including Mr. Owen. We told them: This is a factual situation which requires new crimes or a new war in order to return the Serbs from where they fled and do the same for the Muslims. Let us wait for the end of the war and then everybody will have the right to return to their original places of birth. And we always sustained the position that upon the cessation of war operations, everybody should be given a right to return from where they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So General Mladic came up with this on his own, notwithstanding the comments by Dr. Karadzic reflected in the 46th Session? And the Bosnian Serb leadership did not suggest to him that it would be a good idea to enhance the factual situation so that the negotiations -- the final negotiating position would be better for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is easy to establish that this is not correct. We had 70 per cent of territory. Should we ask for 90 per cent in order to gain a better --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, excuse me. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- position so that we can later claim 50 per cent of the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to establish it by logic. To the extent you were a participant in these events, I want to know if, irrespective of what you claim to be the logic of the situation, whether the Bosnian Serb leadership talked to General Mladic about enhancing the factual situation through military operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask for it. But of course, if you have a bigger territory, you are at an advantage. But nobody aspired to occupy a larger territory in order to achieve a better negotiating position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we just saw at the 34th that General Mladic stated that the army had carried out most of the tasks and the strategic goals set to them. So again, there he's taking the position that he's implementing goals put to him and talking to the political leadership. At the 50th Assembly Session, which is P970, we see at pages 21 through 22 of the English and 17 through 18 of the B/C/S, General Mladic in the course of a long speech talking about the military objectives, he said: "Among other things, the basic objectives of all the mentioned operations are to break and destroy as much of their forces as possible, and thus impose by the force of arms the final settlement of the war on the enemy and place the international community in a position of having to recognise the actual situation in the field and end the war. To ensure as favourable conditions as possible for the state and political leaderships to conduct peace negotiations and achieve the strategic aims of the war." And he continued: "The tasks of the war in this war" -- excuse me, "the task of the army in this war stem from the known six strategic objectives adopted by our Assembly which have not been carried out to the full due to the lack of material and other support." Now, that appears very clearly to be another reflection of General Mladic's express stated position that the army was tasked with implementing the strategic objectives and that it was to achieve as much as possible so that the -- and enhance the actual situation in the field so that the ultimate result for the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Serb political negotiators would be improved. It's still your position that the Bosnian Serb leadership had nothing to do with this perception by General Mladic? They didn't talk to him about implementing the strategic objectives, they didn't encourage him to improve the factual situation through military operations; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am telling you and I'm repeating and claiming that at the time when Mladic held such sizeable territory, we had 70 per cent of the territory. There was no reason for the civilian leadership to issue tasks to the army to occupy additional territories in order to improve our position. The situation was already good. As far as the political leadership is concerned, they persistently maintained the position that the solution had to be reached through negotiation. Now, whether the factual situation was a trump card in our hands, it definitely was, but it was not an imperative given to Mladic to create that. He did create it and ultimately we had a better position than if we had been losers, but he wasn't tasked with military operations in order to achieve a better negotiating position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he wasn't tasked with implementing the strategic objectives and the Bosnian Serb political leadership didn't repeatedly encourage him to implement the strategic objectives or repeatedly remind him about the strategic objectives in the context of upcoming military operations; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategic objectives were a platform for the negotiations and all of our people were aware of the strategic objectives and so did Mladic. He certainly could contribute to the implementation of the strategic objectives in his own way, but the goal of the political leadership was not to take the territory and to force a solution on someone. We couldn't do it and we didn't want to do it. We couldn't because the international community was the mediator and we didn't want to because we knew that in Bosnia, whatever kind of war there was, peace had to be signed among the three sides. Without the agreement of the three sides, it could not be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you yourself -- we looked at what Dr. Karadzic said, we looked at what General Mladic said on a couple of occasions, and you yourself said that the Serbian goal of a united and unique state is something that had to be achieved and that you had a plan which would be realised by political, military, and other means; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that the interpretation was quite confusing. It's not a complaint against the interpreters, but I'm afraid that I might make a mistake and lead you on a wrong trail. One thing is this: If Mladic's goal was to achieve the strategic objectives, he would have taken Sarajevo and the Neretva Valley, he would have reached the sea. None of the goals that we stated, he did not achieve except the corridor, I mean Mr. Mladic. Spontaneously some of that was implemented. Some other areas were liberated, other than those where the strategic objectives were focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in your own trial, Mr. Krajisnik, you were confronted with your remarks at the 18th Session of -- in 1992, when you said: "There is no Serb who doesn't want to live in a united and unique state. It is politically impossible now but we must achieve it. We have our own plan and we shall realise it by political, military, and other means, depending on the situation." And that was put to you at transcript page 25519 through 20 of your trial, and you answered that: "Well, we were at war so, of course, I had to mention war, but I didn't think we had to do this by means of war." And you said: "It's not the factual situation that's important." Correct? That was a position that you took at your own trial. That's what you told the Trial Chamber there, that the factual situation simply wasn't important and your mention of military means to realise the plan was only because the war was in progress?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a single Serb today in Republika Srpska, or rather, at least 90 per cent of Serbs wanted and still want to live together with Serbia. It was like that before and then and always. What is a compromise is Bosnia-Herzegovina as it is today. This leadership tried to pursue realistic policy that was supposed to achieve a compromise, and I said correctly then it's true that the Serbs want to live with Serbia. That was a wish expressed as a sort of plebiscite, but that was not realistic policy. This leadership does not want to pursue unrealistic policy and to oppose the will of the other two ethnic groups and the international community, but wants to achieve a solution. We did realise that through special connections, so it was a compromise rather than the maximum that our people wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krajisnik, I asked you about the factual situation and your claim that it wasn't important and that your explicit reference to military means of attaining the plan was only because of the happenstance that there was a war on. And in your answer you focus exclusively on the goal. I'm focusing on the means of achieving that goal. So is that what you told the Trial Chamber, that the factual situation wasn't important to you and the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I do not understand the question because you're quoting, its translated twice. I'll tell you what I meant and you can fit it wherever you please. War, many MPs and many people believed that something could be gained by war, and we said the factual situation, that's the balance of powers and relations in the world, there are other peoples too. We cannot achieve anything by force; we have to do it through negotiations. That was our policy, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 25520 and 25521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in light of your comments about the role of the strategic objectives, the factual situation, your knowledge of military operations, I think it will be instructive to turn to a contemporaneous account, contemporaneous journal, of meetings that took place between the political and military leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I want to call up 1477. That's one of the war journals that General Mladic kept between 1992 and 1995, and I want to look first at a meeting that took place on the 6th of May, that was just a few days before the 16th Assembly Session when the strategic objectives were annunciated, and that's found at page 256, moving on to -- and 262 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like the parties to discuss with the Registrar to identify the correct pages that have been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This reflects talks with Mr. Karadzic, yourself, General Adzic, and so on. And we see Mr. Karadzic speaking first at what appears to be quite some length, but the portion I wanted to direct your attention to in particular appears toward the bottom of page 258. Incidentally, it appears just after he mentions that: "We were in Graz today for negotiations with the Croats." And he says: "It would be good to carry out the demarcation: (a) in order for us to separate; (b) for us to form a corridor; (c) for the Drina not to be a border; and (d) to reach the coast." So in a meeting with General Mladic and General Adzic and a group of generals, doctor -- along with you, Dr. Karadzic annunciates most of the strategic objectives that will be fully articulated to the Bosnian Serb parliament in a few days; right? And he explains to these generals what at least four of those strategic objectives will be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of Mr. Karadzic presenting our future strategic objectives at this meeting. He informed them about it, so not all but just one part, and that followed after the talks with the Croats, as I recently testified, in Graz.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He's explaining to the military what it would be good to do, how to carry out the demarcation. That's what he's explaining to them, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting with the Croats, we agreed how to carry out the demarcation between us and them. We agreed on that, so it wasn't a task for the military and then told to the Croats. He is presenting what we agreed with the Croats, how to carry out this demarcation between the Croats and us after these talks, in the corridor by an exchange of territories and in the Neretva valley. We also talked about that, where to draw the demarcation line between them and us, the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that had nothing to do with General Mladic's remarks at the 34th, the 50th, and elsewhere, that the strategic objectives were set out to the military and that they indeed accomplished most of them and put the Bosnian Serb leadership in the best negotiating position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they did not achieve most of them. Sarajevo, the Neretva valley, and getting out to the sea, this is what they did not accomplish. But it's normal as the military representatives were at the Assembly. They heard about the objectives, they were announced. Everyone knew that that was our platform for negotiations. There was nothing secret about that. You will remember the Popovic trial where I presented the genesis of the strategic objectives, how they came into being. I submitted it to you and the Tribunal, so I believe that it's not difficult to find them, how the six strategic objectives came into being in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've heard your account of how the strategic objectives came into being, Mr. Krajisnik. And now we're pursuing their role in military operations. The reality is that from the outset, as we see reflected here, the Bosnian Serb leadership told the military what the objectives were and then continued over and over again to remind the military that those were the objectives in the context of upcoming or upcoming military operations or military operations that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did not work towards accomplishing the objectives. I've told you of the six strategic objectives, they never accomplished three. At the same meeting, the session, the 16th one, Mr. Karadzic said: We envisage certain enclaves in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So when the army could liberate territory, it did. And of course, you cannot expect from soldiers not to cherish that. That was their job and they would boast about it, of course, so they would say that that was accomplishing goals, but they didn't accomplish them. Here, specifically, these three objectives were something that they never even tried to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And your testimony is they were just boasting about goals that they came to on their own initiative; it wasn't put to them by the Bosnian Serb political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The six strategic objectives were read out publicly by President Karadzic at the 16th Assembly. On the 9th of June, where Mr. Mladic was, that was a meeting of the Presidency. And then it was said that the strategic objectives should be sent to international representatives, the mediators, as well as our map, and published. So there was no secret about that. And of course, Mladic was aware of the six strategic objectives, but I'm telling you specifically, he liberated the territories he could but he wasn't taking into account the strategic objectives nor were they any kind of obligation for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We -- well, let's look at a meeting the next day, on May 7th, and in particular, let's -- I want to remind you of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, that you didn't remember meeting with General Mladic, and if you did, you certainly didn't discuss any goals with him. So let's turn now to page -- that's 1477 again, page 260 -- sorry, 262 in both languages. This is yet another meeting with you and Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. And there -- I'm sorry, it's B/C/S page 270. Generally these conform. Meeting of 7 May at 1600 hours, right. At that meeting, Mr. Krajisnik, you annunciated in full the strategic objectives to General Mladic, to separate from the Croats and Muslims forever, to make a corridor from Krajina to Serbia, to establish a link with Serbia on the Drina and cut off the Muslims' link, a natural border with the Croats on the Neretva, Sarajevo, and passage to the sea. So for two days, you and Dr. Karadzic met with General Mladic and on both days ensured that he was fully conversant with the strategic objectives? And you -- correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have just forgotten that I said here that we do not want to live alone. I'm not sure if I said that too, but here this is correct -- I mean correct. I want to say that -- I want to confirm that what I'm reading here is correct. Now, whether this is just what he wrote, I don't know. He says that Krajisnik enumerated the strategic goals and there are seven goals here, like in the near future we must -- I'm not sure what follows then after that. And during my testimony here I said that perhaps I or Mr. Karadzic may have formulated it, but you can see from what was said on the previous day was that Mr. Karadzic actually listed some goals. So he may have put that it was me and it could have been our joint agreement or it's possible that he attended a meeting on which the strategic goals that would be prepared for the Assembly were presented, and the Assembly was to be held in the next several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, there are not seven goals listed. You can see that he's got a line identifying the six goals and then he moves on with an asterisk to talk about the discussion: We do not want to live alone. In the near future, you are recorded as relating to him, we want to establish links with the RSK. The latter point of which was a continuing point of interest by the Bosnian Serb leadership, to unite with the RSK. In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, this entry reflects the obvious, that Mr. Mladic -- that General Mladic, as he's about to assume his responsibilities, is being told what his objectives are to be? And one more thing -- you answer that and I'll ask you the next one.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not giving tasks to Mr. Mladic by telling him the goals because he was not yet the commander. We didn't know when he would become the commander. This is probably, though I don't know, a conversation with a number of participants where the strategic objectives were conceived as a platform for talks, a platform that we would advocate and that would be announced to the Assembly. So these were not tasks issued to General Mladic. He was still to become the commander. These were talks. The talks could have been held with anyone else in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it doesn't -- this could have been anybody. The fact that it's General Mladic is irrelevant or coincidental. That's your position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the previous meeting was held with the generals from Bosnia-Herzegovina, with Mr. Adzic, so we issued tasks to them too. They had nothing to do with Mladic and the future Army of Republika Srpska. I'm telling you one thing, these were the political objectives which were conceived here, and Mladic could be aware of them. Why shouldn't he be familiar with them? But these were not his tasks or orders issued to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you did not say to General Mladic on the 7th of May with regard to strategic objective number 3: Our goal is to establish a border control station on the Drina that will not ask for passports, but will accept visas? That wasn't your articulation of strategic objective number 3 on the 7th of May, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please bring it back, the strategic objectives, so I can see how exactly the third strategic objective was formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 270, I believe, in the B/C/S and page 260 in -- excuse me, 262 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always advocated that the Drina should not be a border at which passports needed to be shown, and I quoted what Mr. Izetbegovic himself had said. We always applied for this and it was always approved by international community representatives, namely, to have special and parallel relations and that exists to this day. Today, you don't have to show a passport but only the personal identity card. That was the goal, not to have a unification of Republika Srpska and Serbia, but that the border is a soft one which can easily be crossed as people do it today within the EU.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But that's not what you said to General Mladic on the 7th of May. You didn't say: We want a soft border that can be easily crossed by people. You said you wanted to cut off the Muslims' link with Sandzak and establish a link with Serbia on the Drina. Would a soft border, Mr. Krajisnik, cut off the link with the Sandzak? It would seem to me it would enhance it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the Drina is not the border with Sandzak. The Drina is the border with Serbia proper, and Mladic could have noted this in the way he wanted to. He may have included some of his own reminiscences. I always advocated - I'm not sure about how that's portrayed here - as what we negotiated with the Muslims in the talks with them and also with international community; namely, that it should be a border where we wouldn't have border posts and passports, but one that would be easy to cross and go over and it exists today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, if I may help. In line 12, though I see that it's noted, his "reminiscences" is what's missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I can continue, Mr. President, but it looks like we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It's time for another break. We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Ms. Milica Milicevic, who was originally from Serbia but grew up in the United Kingdom and is now studying here in the Netherlands and working as a legal intern for our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue, I would like to ask -- inquire of the parties about the scheduling. In the week of 9th of December, whether it would cause a lot of problems if we are to sit from Tuesday to Friday instead of Monday to Thursday? We are supposed to sit from 9th to 12th. I'm inquiring whether it would be possible to sit from the 10th to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the past such requests have not presented any problems so we will check and get back to you very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It won't be a problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next, Mr. Krajisnik, to some of the directives that were issued before military operations. As we've heard in this chamber, a directive is a high command document which addresses broad issues of preparation and execution of military operations for an extended period, setting out goals and tasks. And I'd like to start with the first directive which was dated the 6th of June, 1992, and that's D232. Now if we turn to the second page of the English and we look under the goal of the operation, that appears immediately after 4, you'll see it at the bottom of your page and then continuing on into the second page of B/C/S. It states: "Secure parts of Sarajevo with a majority Serbian population to ocistiti /mop up or cleanse/ the wider area of Sarajevo airport and ocistiti its wider area of remaining groups and of individuals belonging to the enemy ..." et cetera. And if we turn to the item after item (D), we see that the directive provides: "In the first stage, in duration of 3 to 4 days, use offensive actions to ocistiti the wider sector around Sarajevo airport (Dobrinja, Butmir, Sokolovic, Kolonija, Mojmilo, Zlatiste), deblock the communication," et cetera, "Sarajevo-Trnovo and group forces to open the corridor between Semberija and Bosnian Krajina." And again immediately below: "In the second stage, in duration of 4 to 6 days, create the corridor between Semberija and Bosnian Krajina, reject enemy forces away from the communications, and in the period to come, extend the corridor permanently providing secure traffic communication in it." And again, Mr. Krajisnik, we see here the term "ocistiti" and in English the two possible translations for that, depending on the context in which it appears, are provided and this Court has heard evidence - that's found at 14572 through 14575 - that the term sometimes appears in a military context referring to the mopping up of the terrain, a military term for the final stages of the operation, or may refer to a cleansing which may in context mean the removal of the population. So it's in this document in the English translation left with both possibilities and the original word in Serbian is inserted. But with respect to the items I identified for you, do we see here in the first directive and in the fairly early stage of the VRS's involvement in the conflict a reflection of two of the strategic objective and an attempt to produce a factual situation which can support various demands during negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert so it's hard for me to interpret this. Anything that I would interpret would be arbitrary and certainly not of a very high quality. What I can say now as a lay person is the following. I can say that at the time our ethnic areas were split up, disjointed, and it is certain that the actual situation on the ground made it necessary to link certain things up. It says here ethnic areas around Sarajevo where Serbs were the prevalent population. Also, it has to do with this linking up by way of communication. I could not say that this is linked to the strategic objectives or this strategic objective. Quite simply, the situation was such that it made it necessary to link areas up in the eastern part. As for this reference to the corridor, you know that -- here in the documents you see that the entire western part of Krajina was isolated because of humanitarian aid, that was a particular problem. And to this day there is a monument to 12 babies that died due to a lack of oxygen, and there was a lot of pressure then to open this humanitarian corridor towards the western part of Republika Srpska, which was done afterwards. So I don't see anything unusual here in this military document, and I as a layman again, I could not link this up to ethnic cleansing. It is actually the military that is mopping up and it says here "enemy," and the enemy is the enemy soldiers on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those actions that were reflected in the directive were the result of meetings with the Bosnian Serb political leadership, including yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is the 6th of June, as far as I can remember, the first meeting of the expanded Presidency was on the 9th of June, that is to say, it was later. I don't know whether there was a meeting before that, say an informal meeting, unrecorded. But as far as I can remember, the first meeting with Mr. Mladic was on the 9th of June, that is to say, three days before this directive was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Take a look at P1478, page 92, a meeting held on the 5th of June, 1992, involving General Mladic, yourself, Koljevic, Plavsic, and Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the date here. Can you tell me where the date is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a meeting that took place at 1600 hours, so the date is reflected at an earlier portion of the document and is 5 June. If you wish to scroll back, we can do so; if you take my word for it, we can do so. Also on the very next page we see the entry of 6th of June and you'll see that in a moment. So you'll see that it moves from 1600 hours on this date to the 6th of June on the very next entry. And General Mladic writes down "demands" as after -- that arise from his meeting with the political leadership. "To liberate the road going through Zlatiste; "To occupy the border in the city and to reinforce it; "The issue of our objective in Sarajevo. Sarajevo has to be resolved politically while acting quietly inch by inch" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. We move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And "ocistiti," mop up or cleanse, "Butmir, Hrasnica, Dobrinja, and Sokolovic Kolonija, and in the town of Hrasno in the direction of Mojmilo hill." Here, Mr. Krajisnik, we see the demand, as it says here, arising from the meeting of the state and political leadership, and in particular you and Dr. Karadzic, to do precisely what is reflected in the -- in directive 1 on June 6th; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this exactly is confirmation that it has to do with communication, I mean this talk. I didn't know that there would be a directive afterwards, I certainly didn't know, but I do not exclude the possibility of this meeting being held and this being discussed. I don't remember exactly whether the meeting was a meeting of the Presidency or some other meeting, but I do not rule out the possibility of such problems being discussed because it says here "Sarajevo has to be resolved by political means," but of course; Zlatiste, where the road had been cut off; also at the airport where they're firing at those who are bringing in humanitarian aid; and then Trnovo, all of this is discussion about communication. It is only natural that a directive would follow after certain talks. I don't remember this being said. I don't see anything strange here and I allow for the possibility of this kind of meeting having been held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll check the transcript, but perhaps I misunderstood you earlier when you were telling this Chamber over and over again that the operations of the VRS had nothing to do with the political leadership. So now I understand from you that it's natural that specific military operations and military directives would arise immediately in the aftermath of the meeting with the political leadership and based on what the political leadership said about what needed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand what it is that is not understandable. I'll try to explain, and if that is not in accordance with what I had said, then you have the possibility of saying that I haven't been consistent. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What I want to know from you is specifically now whether or not it's your position that military operations were the result of meetings with and instructions from the Bosnian Serb political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you want to get an answer through this play of words. I am telling you that if you get that, that is wrong, and I'll try to explain things if something is unclear to you. I said that there were very few meetings with the military, and for the most part what was discussed was logistics. There was information, certain information, of course, and we discussed certain problems too, but that was not obligatory in terms of issuing orders to the military. From the ground there were certain requests, certain wishes, but it wasn't demands of the civilian authorities. The planning of the military was autonomous and nobody had to tell them what to do and how to resolve things because they would see the situation on the ground specifically here. If this conversation did take place, and I assume that it did take place, it is only natural that we had this discussion with Mladic about the problems related to Sarajevo, for example, this and that and the other thing is a problem, and then after that what he's going to do and whether he's going to do it. That was not a request. That was simply a discussion about problems that have to do with the situation on the ground. If it is not clear from this, then you can put additional questions to me and I can give you an answer. This is a meeting that did not have to be a pretext for the directive. It could have been so but it was not obligatory for the military. There's going to be another meeting, say, there was a meeting on the 9th of June, and I don't know whether there was a directive that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at a meeting that took place the next day, June 6th. There we see consultations on the military and political situation, that's the date of the issuance of the directive. Item 4 is: "The political and military doctrine for upcoming war objectives." And Dr. Karadzic speaks and, as we see toward the bottom of the page on 94, Dr. Karadzic "reiterated the strategic objectives with comments and explanations." And he ends by saying: "We have to protect our territories militarily." So now for the fourth time in approximately a month, that being May 6th, May 7th, May 12th, and now June 6th, the Bosnian Serb political leadership is emphasising the strategic objectives to General Mladic, this time in the specific context of a discussion on the political and military doctrine for upcoming war objectives.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a consultative meeting of soldiers, and it is only natural that politicians were present there. Mr. Karadzic is saying what the political objectives are. It is the Assembly that adopted these political objectives. I don't know whether what Mr. Mladic said here is correct, verbatim. He said that the army is supposed to protect our territories. I don't see that he said: Let's take somebody else's territories. Well, of course, what do we need an army for if it's not going to protect our territories?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you don't see a reference to Dr. Karadzic saying: Let's take somebody else's territories or let's conquer somebody else's territories? That's what you're saying that this meeting is about only?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying I don't know what the content is of what Mladic wrote down. I know that at such consultative meetings it is a particular subject matter that is discussed. It says here that we have to protect our territories in a military way --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he says here the situation is very unfavourable. You see that that's what he wrote down. I don't know whether what he wrote down is correct, but I'm telling you what it is that I am reading right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at who did state that what needed to happen was that the army had to conquer what the Bosnian Serbs considered theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 108, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That reflects your contributions to this meeting toward the end of the meeting and you say the following: "The goal was to form and unite the Birac-Romanija area. "To draw the borders of this area and to include: Hadzici, Ilidza, Vojkovici, and Novo Sarajevo. "Dobrinja, if we can take it. "Those who liberated Hadzici, Vogosca ... this should be defended, that will be ours. "The border has to be defended and held". And we turn to the next page, 108. "As of tomorrow we have to conquer what is ours and be prepared to defend our state ..." So that's what the Bosnian Serb leadership was telling the VRS, immediate -- yes, contemporaneous with the issuance of directive 6?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said then I would say today as well, all of these areas are Serb areas, and I did not say that a single foot of Muslim territory should be taken. I said that our territory should be protected, and that is the views of the participants in a particular meeting. It would be very naive to say that Momcilo Krajisnik in this way gave a task, an order, to the military. I said, as a participant, I said what should belong to us around Sarajevo. Our territory, to take up lines and to defend it. I did not say that Bascarsija should be taken. I did not say that Butmir should be taken. I did not say that the inner city of Sarajevo should be taken. Rather, only that that belonged to the Serb people ethnically. I followed that, that we had already charted as our areas with Mr. Cutileiro on the maps there. This is not a directive, this is not a proposal; this is the opinion of a participant, the Speaker of the Assembly, addressing a broader forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your words were that: "As of tomorrow we have to conquer" -- you weren't saying to take or liberate territory that was not then being held by the Bosnian Serbs, you weren't saying conquer territory already had. You were saying conquer territory that was held by the Muslims, but that you considered to be -- that you considered the Serbs entitled to; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. Do read this. I don't know whether that's the word I uttered, but it says here exactly "our territories," "our," and they're listed too. I did not say "our Butmir." I did not say "our Bascarsija." That would mean that we were aspiring for something that was held by the Muslims and that was their own. The Muslim side held some of our territory, so what we are alluding to is that these territories should be freed because that's where Serbs are. According to the maps they belonged to us and they belong to us today on the basis of the Dayton Agreement, too. As for the word "conquer," I don't know why that word was used. Maybe he put that, if that's a military term. I may have used the word "osloboditi," to liberate, but why would I say "conquer"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And once again we see the -- in your words, desires or wishes of the Bosnian Serb leadership reflected in the directives guiding military operations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been honoured if anyone took heed of my wishes, any wishes, let's say in inverted commas. There were several participants they -- and it doesn't mean that what Krajisnik said we are going to incorporate in the directive and then we move on. It might have happened accidentally that I mentioned something that I wouldn't say today. I said that we need to liberate the Serbian areas, they need to be connected and linked up, because somebody had occupied these areas. I didn't say these territories had to be cleansed, but I said that they needed to be liberated because they had been occupied by someone and it's only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next to directive 3 issued in August. That's D235. And -- and perhaps before we look at that in detail, maybe we can look at a couple of documents that indicate what happened between directive 1 on June 6th, 1992, and the directive 3 on the 3rd of August, 1992. So if we could turn to directive 2 on -- which is D593 first, please. And sorry to the Registrar for jumping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is dated July 22nd, 1992, and it indicates in the informative section of the directive at the beginning in one of the two items indicated as item 1, the second of those two items: "We liberated the territories we consider ours and created conditions for political and military leadership of the Serbian Republic of BiH, so that they could perform all activities and negotiations regarding the future state of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the position of the stronger one in this territory." Item 4: "We have broken through corridors in Eastern Bosnia and Bosanska Posavina and thus made possible the centuries-long aspiration of the Serbian people from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbian Republic of Krajina to be joined with the fatherland - Serbia." And item 7: "We have created conditions for further progress of our army and state in this territory." So that document in the latter part of July 1992, directive 2, reflects, first of all, the attainment of the corridors in Eastern Bosnia and Bosanska Posavina, those are two of the strategic objectives that were articulated to General Mladic four times before the first week -- or by the first week of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the corridor in Posavina was one of the strategic objectives and the linking up of the area along the Drina was another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it reflects the military's understanding that the liberation of territories that we consider to be ours, that is, that the Bosnian Serbs consider to be theirs, created conditions for the political and military leadership so that they could perform all activities regarding the future state and be in the position of the stronger one on the territory; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that is how I think that the army understood, as it is written in this directive. Of course they were familiar with those objectives and they interpreted them as they saw fit. Nobody told them explicitly what to do. The entire nation was in favour of opening up the Krajina in order to get medical supplies in, in order to prevent the death of infants. It wasn't necessary to tell them anything. If anyone did tell them, though, it just was consistent with the situation. It has nothing to do with the objectives, which was dictated by the prevailing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I wanted to turn to directive 3 which was the previous document, D00235. So now we have some understanding of what happened in the interim, and we see in directive 3, first, there is a general political background provided in paragraph 1, and it notes in -- at page 2 that the army has achieved significant results in protecting the Serbian people and their centuries-old home. But let's look at the objectives for the future and the tasks which are provided by directive 3. First of all, it seeks to keep Sarajevo firmly under blockade and prevent its breaking. It, once again, mentions - this is page 3 in both languages - advancing to the left bank of the river Neretva, the right bank of the river Sava, and border areas of Serbian territories, capture Jajce and Gorazde, take hold of dominant features and ensure the most favourable possible position in the negotiations with the Croat-Muslim alliance on demarcation. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then the document continues to make specific assignments to various corps in the pursuit of these objectives. Now, once again, Mr. Krajisnik, we see reflected in this directive, the reference to the Neretva, the reference to the Sava, the reference to liberating remaining parts of Serbian territory, reflections of strategic objective number 4, strategic objective number 2, strategic objective number 1, general separation, in the guiding documents for military operations by the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not correct. Let me tell you why. Because the strategic objectives were not made up. They rely on realistic foundations to what we were entitled to, and we had the right to each of these strategic objectives. So if something is realistic and if none of these objectives were adopted, then the Serbian army had -- would have had a right to liberate the areas where the Serbs had been living. I don't know how it all went on, how these directives were formulated, but I can say that the six strategic objectives was a political document known to everyone, including the army, and anyone was free to invoke them. Everyone had the right to defend themselves. There is not a single objective that aspires to grabbing somebody else's territory; it was not incorporated in our objectives. We only claimed what we thought we had a right to, the access to sea, the Neretva Valley where the Serbs used to live and were subjected to genocide. So we aspired to everything that was allowed by the Cutileiro Plan. It was only natural for the army to know what the objectives were and what they were supposed to do as part of their task. But it was not that the leadership said: Let us do this in a military way, although we don't have a right to do that, in order to gain a better negotiating position. Our position was very favourable and we continued the negotiations. Precisely on the 7th of August, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic signed a declaration with Mr. Hurd in London, where it said that all the areas that are taken by force was something that we were opposed to and each such territory had to be returned. Now this is construed in a different way, that we are trying to occupy territories in order to improve our political position. We were constantly striving for a political solution and the policy-makers said we want something that we're entitled to. The Serbs can claim 65 per cent of the territory, mostly rural territory, not urban territory. And this was publicly made known. However, we did not achieve everything because the Dayton Accords provided different solutions, so it was not feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said: "I don't know how it all went on, how these directives were formulated," and then you went on to offer the long explanation about strategic objectives that you just did. So in connection with how this directive came about, let's look first at P3068, which was a meeting of the Presidency one day before directive 3 was issued. And we see that the second item on the agenda is the assessment of the military situation. And if we turn the page we can see that General Mladic briefed those present on the assessment of the military situation in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, describing the situation in each combat sector, the necessary tasks, and the connection between ensuring material potentials and financial resources, and the necessity of adopting a decision on general mobilisation due to security considerations, and the detailed nature of the information, the conclusions, and alternatives adopted were not put on record. And this is another meeting with General Mladic that you participated in, as we see from the notation indicating who the session was attended by. Okay? So this was, as it states here, a briefing on the situation in each sector and what needed to be done next; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is exactly what I have been saying all the time. Read this item consistently. Mr. Mladic briefed the president about the situation on the ground, and we all know that from TV. Then he spoke about the material support that was required for the army to be capable of combat, and that was the point of every meeting that I attended where Mr. Mladic was present. There was not a single meeting where some different issues were discussed. What they discussed was something that I saw on TV as well. Of course he provided more detailed explanations and he said in order for us to be able to continue our activities, and every soldier is proud of what he is doing, he would say: We need ammunition, we need food, we need uniforms, et cetera, et cetera. So that was our activity. And although these meetings were far and few between, whenever I was present this is what Mladic talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So what you all knew from TV had to not be put on the record due to security considerations; that's the first thing, right? That's what the record of the meeting reflects, that what you say everybody could see on TV was not put on the record due to security considerations; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we all served in the army. Whenever an army wants to do something significant, they say: This is a military secret. This is a state secret. In order to create in the minds of people who are present there that they were keeping something to themselves. I never heard in any of the meetings anything that could be treated as a special military secret. Many people didn't know what was happening on the ground during the war, and I'm telling you that that is the real truth and it's wrong to see that somebody was making a mystery of the whole situation. Of course, soldiers are the most important factor in war and, of course, they try to give more importance to themselves, but I really convinced you that I never heard anything that was top secret, that there was a crime that had been committed and somebody tried to cover it up. All of us who served in the army know that this is the truth. The army always tries to say that there is something very important and that shouldn't be disseminated among the people and that it should be publicised only on a need-to-know basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to another reflection of the meeting on the 2nd of August and that's found at P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, this is not a military document, is it? This is a minute from the Presidency meeting, probably kept by a civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it says here what was said at that time. Maybe Mr. Mladic said: Don't put that on paper, but if something important was said - and I don't remember that there was anything important - wasn't important enough to be put on record. You can see that there are so many things that are contained in the minutes because they were more important. There were many security issues during the war. This culture of security awareness did not exist too much among us because it is possible that he didn't write everything down, so I conclude that if he omitted to write it down, it wasn't significant enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's turn next to P1479, English pages 16 through 23 -- well, in this case both languages. As a general matter, the Serbian and the English will track in this document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a reflection of that same meeting, a meeting on the 2nd of August, 1992, with the Presidency, as reflected in General Mladic's diary. We see essentially the same agenda: "Briefing on the talks in London (Karadzic). "Assessment of the military situation. "Plan for future activities." And as we continue through the document, we see a fairly lengthy discussion of various aspects. We see at the end something that will come up in another document. Mr. Koljevic saying: "To take Sarajevo. "To launch a sabotage operation," that's on page 23, "and eliminate the political leadership." So toward the end of this discussion on the assessment of the military situation and plan for future activities, Mr. Koljevic offers that contribution. And prior to that we see on page 22, let's go to page 21 first, look at the bottom. After you say: "We must raise the issue of our access to the sea ..." Then on the next page, page 22, we see that Dr. Karadzic says: "The European Community will accept the factual state of affairs, and that is why we should not make a single concession in military terms." So that's another reflection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is it Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand the confusion, Mr. President, but you see -- look immediately to the right and upwards, it looks like the reference for Karadzic and in the -- as you can see in the Serbian, it's less confusingly listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's another reflection of the Bosnian Serb leadership saying to General Mladic exactly what he said at the 34th Assembly Session and the 50th Assembly Session and in any number of military directives that we've seen, is that he understood the role of the military in part to be obtaining a factual situation on the ground that would enhance the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often information from the West, from our conferences, came that an agreement cannot be reached, that representatives of the international community wanted certain area to be given over to another ethnic community, and that created chaos because huge areas became vacant. Why should any territory be conceded to another ethnic community? People who liberated certain area and the political leadership, which was particularly emphasised by Mr. Karadzic as the president of the party, used to say that whatever we occupied, the international community must acknowledge that. For example, we took Gorazde, somebody said Gorazde will be given to the Muslims and people just packed and left. Some of them were slaughtered. Only three or four days later Mr. Karadzic signed a paper which said that we were ready to make territorial concessions only with a view to reaching a political solution. If he says that publicly in an international conference, then the ordinary people say: Look, they're bargaining there. Why should we wage war? Why should we liberate areas that are going to be given to the other side anyway? It is only natural that there are talks during a war with the military and some other people, but these were not directives. These were not orders. This was just a discussion that every civilian was involved in. The army was doing its job professionally, and in view of the factual situation they acted accordingly. If they can liberate something, they resorted to that. As I said, they didn't take the Neretva Valley, they didn't take Sarajevo. It was mentioned a hundred times, but it was not a goal. They didn't take Sarajevo, but they did take Jajce, though, although we said it's not going to be ours. According to the maps, it should have belonged to the Muslim-Croat Federation. I understand what you are trying to prove here, that is to say, that the political leadership in the meetings that I attended was involved in the discussions about the problems, and the only real problem was the war, the people being killed, the refugees, et cetera. We discussed that, but these were not orders, these were wishes. They were suggestions passed on to the army that waged the war as best they could. They were sometimes successful, sometimes unsuccessful. I don't say that there were no directives that the Commander-in-Chief issued and he co-ordinated that with his Main Staff, but I don't know anything about these directives. Some things happened spontaneously and chaotically on the ground. I can give you a hundred examples of things that took us by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you look at the balance of powers in certain municipalities and if you see that people native to that area took part in the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, let's look at two more documents to see how spontaneous or chaotic this directive was. So first let's look at P3069, another session of the Presidency two days later on August 4th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous answer it turns out that -- it was omitted that there were municipal armies, and I'm talking about line 8 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. There we see, on the 4th, the Presidency considered the -- and again, this is a meeting which you attended, as we see reflected at the outset of the meeting. The document also reflects that the Presidency considered the situation at the front and discussed undertaking certain activities at the front. Now, those activities at the front meant directive 3, and that's what the Presidency considered and that's, in fact, what was approved by the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see here that directive 3 is mentioned anywhere. Can you please tell me where you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were present at that meeting. So I'm asking you when we see the reference to what the Presidency considered and discussed at that meeting, that that's a reference to directive 3 and that, in fact, the Presidency approved directive 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't, Mr. Tieger. I never heard that I needed to adopt a directive at the Presidency. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P1479, English pages -- beginning at page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is another entry in General Mladic's diary, this time reflecting the same meeting with the Presidency that was held on the 4th of August -- or reflecting a meeting with the Presidency on the 4th of August, 1992. And as we can see at the very beginning: "Directive accepted without objections, except for Koljevic who requested the following: "(a)," and that's the same thing he talked about on August 2nd, "a sabotage operation in Sarajevo. "(b) the taking of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was presented like this and that someone mentioned the directive. Perhaps we talked about some -- the meeting was held, we discussed, but that somebody said: Let us adopt a directive now, I never heard something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the previous document. Was Mladic noted as one of the participants?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe he's listed as a participant in that particular meeting. I will note -- could ask Mr. Krajisnik this question, in fact, if I can find the particular transcript page -- no, he's not listed as attending that particular meeting. So I -- I will note that -- and I'll find the reference and ask Mr. Krajisnik about it, that he made a point in his previous testimony of noting that not every participant in the meeting was always listed on the Presidency session minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next, Mr. Krajisnik, to directive 4 and that's dated November 19th, 1992. That's P00976. And I'd like to look at that before turning your attention to some other meetings. Now, if we look at page 2 in both languages, we can see, among other things, that the 1st Krajina Corps has preserved and expanded the borders of Republika Srpska. It also indicates at item 6 that the Drina Corps was formed. It indicates, on the third page in English, the tasks from directive 3 that have not yet been carried out; that is, that the towns of Gorazde, Gradacac, Maglaj, Bugojno, Olovo, and Orasje have not been liberated. It indicates that the Posavina corridor has not been substantially widened. Enemy groups in the wider area of Gorazde, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Cerska have not been totally routed. "The Herzegovina Corps has failed to reach the left bank of Neretva river and secure access ..." Looking down on the paragraph below that, in item 4 we again see the instruction to: "Create conditions for the state leadership of Republika Srpska to participate equally in resolving the Crisis Staff in the former BH with other international factors." So just in this brief review of those portions of directive 4, we again see reflections of the focus on the Posavina corridor, the Neretva River, access to the sea, among others, that is, numbers of the strategic objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's mentioned here is a number of towns, Orasje, Bugojno, and so on. None of these towns are included in the strategic objectives. It was simply that the army, depending on the terrain -- the army included it in the directive. And the three strategic objectives that you mentioned, the corridor, Sarajevo, and coming out to sea and Neretva, those were the political goals that we were entitled to and they were familiar to anyone. And of course the army mentions them too. I don't see anything strange in that, but none of them were accomplished. The corridor was but it was not expanded. It remained 3 kilometres throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, didn't the Bosnian Serb leadership prior to the issuance of this directive - and by the Bosnian Serb leadership, in particular I mean Dr. Karadzic and you - remind General Mladic and the VRS of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we -- I apologise. May I? May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And of course, by that I mean in the context of discussions about upcoming military operations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible that in some conversation the strategic objectives were mentioned, at a meeting or at a parliament session, because they were generally known. Those were the political objectives that were an obligation for all the people because we would accomplish that politically if we talked and negotiated and so on. The army at the local level, as everyone else, had its own wish to liberate a part of the territory where other members of our people lived and no one could deny them that if they had enough power. But the political goal and objective was not to take other people's territories but only those spaces where ethnic Serbs lived. So it's possible that it may have been mentioned, but it wasn't an order or a threat to the effect that if you don't do that, there will be sanctions against you; or if you fail to do it as a soldier, you will not accomplish the strategic objectives. That's simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about some incidental or peripheral mention of the strategic objectives. I'm talking about focusing on the need to apply military resources to the political -- to the strategic objectives and, indeed, let's say to certain strategic objectives as opposed to others. That's what the Bosnian Serb leadership did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 times there was discussion about the need to come out to the Neretva or to the sea or that we should get a part of Sarajevo, but that was a political objective that we mentioned in negotiations. No one said: Let us take all of Sarajevo. Let us take -- or where are the borders of Neretva or let us take all of Neum, no. What we once presented at international community negotiations is what was mentioned after that. It is completely normal that we said wherever it was: Look, those are the strategic objectives. It is not Gradacac or Tuzla, which are not ours, but those are the strategic objectives where the Serbs live and where the international mediators have an understanding about this whenever we had negotiations and contacts with them. And that's the whole truth. And the army was supposed to hold the lines reached, which the local units had liberated because we didn't have the solutions. If we did, we would have applied immediately the map we had where we were supposed to return 30 per cent of territory. You have documents about that. I cannot tell you this on top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can go to item 5(d) of this directive, that's the third-to-the-last page in Serbian and the fifth page in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you just scroll down a bit, please, because I don't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the paragraph that begins with "Drinski Korpus ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone could read it out because I really can't read what's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not right page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm told that there is a better or more readable version of this attached to the same document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see the correct page first. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm told if we go to the back of the -- the third-to-last page of this entire document, it contains a more readable version in Serbian of the portion in question. You can see it here, it's not that hard to read, but I'm told it's better to -- there you go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that particular section of directive 4 reads as follows: "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces are to defend with utmost persistence Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them, and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas with the Muslim population ..." Now, that's a criminal order, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me such a question during my trial, and by your suggestion, I confirmed this when reading this. However, later on I talked with the author of this directive, Mr. Miletic, who said that he didn't know how such an error could have crept on him. I don't think that it's decent for me to interpret somebody's thoughts. There are people here who can interpret what they wrote. I have seen a hundred times that when something is written, perhaps one single word which would allow a different interpretation may have been omitted. So I cannot confirm what I said once when you suggested to me whether this is correct, yes. If someone said that somebody should be cleansed from a territory, I would say that it is criminal, but I'm not sure if this is correct. You should ask Mr. Miletic or whoever else wrote this in the directive. He didn't tell me that it was criminal, but he told me he wondered that it was formulated as this. He told me in the DU while I was there, and I asked him because I commented on this very vehemently when this was presented to me, just like now, by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, I didn't present that to you, Judge Orie did. And what happened at pages 25605 to 25607 is that you read this portion of directive 4 and then you started explaining, as you were discussing the directive, that you were deeply against ethnic cleansing. And so Judge Orie asked you: "Well, do you consider this to be an order for ethnic cleansing?" To which you said: "Absolutely, yes." So your characterisation of, your interpretation of, your understanding of this directive was not at my suggestion. It was based on a question of the Judge, prompted by your assertions regarding ethnic cleansing. And that's the truth of what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
