utterances.text: I'm sorry if I blame you and you are not to blame because it turns out that in my case you are only to blame, I mean the Prosecutors. I'm sorry if Judge Orie did that. But anyway, my answer would be the same. I'm sorry that now I have to object against him. I was interpreting what I see written here, and later I talked with Mr. Miletic and I saw that I really took it on myself to interpret something where I was not right because I took it at face value. And I could see this happen in many other instances where you suggested something, probably it was just an extract, and then the one who provided an answer gave a wrong one because the person was not qualified enough to interpret something. What he meant by "cleanse" or not, the one who really wrote it should interpret it. It's really indecent for me to say literally that it is so, and I did say that previously in my own case, I did say: Yes, you are right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Directive 4, and in particular the portions of directive 4, including this instruction to the Drina Corps, didn't come out of the blue to General Mladic. It came after he was repeatedly reminded by the Bosnian Serb leadership of the need to separate from Muslims, of the risk that Muslims might otherwise become a majority, and of the insistence that clearing the Drina area was the most important task. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic never received a request from us to ethnically cleanse the Drina and this area, that's not correct. And you can see how many public statements of Mr. Karadzic you have here and other leaders, to the effect that they oppose ethnic cleansing. And in every agreement we took on us the obligation that everyone should return to their homes. And since the 27th of March, before the war, Mr. Karadzic was saying: We allow for enclaves to exist in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim enclaves, and our policy - I'm telling you what our policy was - it was to establish our own Republika Srpska. And according to the Cutileiro Plan, it meant an internal demarcation within Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to form three ethnic constitutive units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know you want to talk about what was publicly said. Right now I'm interested in what was said to General Mladic in meetings that weren't available to the public. So I asked you if it wasn't the case that General Mladic was reminded of the need to separate from Muslims, the risk that Muslims might otherwise become a majority if that separation didn't take place, and of the -- and reminded and indeed of the Bosnian Serb political leadership's position that clearing the Drina area was the most important or among the most important of upcoming tasks, not what was said to the public.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand this question as several questions. I will try to answer as I have understood it. Ethnic cleansing was not our policy. No one ever issued Mladic the task to ethnically cleanse Eastern Bosnia. Secondly, as for separation, separation was one of the main principles of the Cutileiro Plan and all other plans, in order to form constituent units. That was normal. And thirdly, in each plan there was an obligation for all parties, all sides, including the Serbian one, with regard to refugees who had left their areas, that they are to be able to return, and we all opposed the idea that territories taken by force could be a final solution in any plan nor would we acknowledge that. You will find it in the platform dated at 22nd of April, 1992, issued by Mr. Karadzic and on many other occasions it was stated publicly. What is secret, as you said? I really don't know if there was a meeting. I want to be precise. A secret meeting at which someone said: Let us now expel these people from such and such an area. I don't know. You've seen how many telephone conversations were recorded. It should have been mentioned in some telephone conversation if it was unlawful that Momcilo Krajisnik or Radovan Karadzic said: Let's expel somebody, or somebody may have been angry because we are temperamental, we are such people, but you cannot find it anywhere. So this would be my answer to your long question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P01479, page 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look at two of the meetings which preceded the issuance of directive 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 19 what is missing: [In English] But you cannot find it anywhere to be part of policy. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a military political consultation meeting held on the 2nd of September, 1992, with a briefing by the commanders of the corps, various corps. And as we go through the document, page 132, we see the -- one of the corps commanders talking about weaponry, a briefing by the 2nd Krajina Corps on page 134; the Eastern Bosnia Corps on 135; the Herzegovina Corps on 136. And beginning on page 140, you speak. And first you express a concern with criticism of the SDS, what you call the movement which brought people together. And then you go on at page 143 to explain: "Our aim is to divide with the Muslims. If the Muslims were to capitulate, we would remain with them. If they remained with us, they would soon be the majority." And then on the next page, once again, you remind the military figures, the VRS, the corps commanders in this case and General Mladic, of the strategic aims: Number 1, "dividing with the Croats and Muslims." Number 2, "the corridor." Number 3, "Sarajevo divided." Number 4, and these are now out of order, "Serbs in the Drina Valley." "5, border on the Neretva and exit to the sea." So once again in the context of a military meeting at which the corps commanders were explaining the situation in their sectors, you took it upon yourself to again remind them of the strategic objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it would be good if that were so because I recall that we didn't need to go to take Tuzla, Gradacac or Bugojno or territories --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, sorry, I don't want the explanation why you would or wouldn't have, according to you. I want to know if you dispute this entry and say you didn't describe the strategic -- annunciate the strategic objectives to the military on September 2nd, or if you confirm that you did?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I believe I did. I don't know that now, but I believe I did. And I don't think it's anything bad nor did I divulge a secret. Everyone knew that because the strategic objectives were public, public knowledge. Each soldier knew it because it was publicly announced and given to the international community, those objectives. I don't see why I wouldn't say: Those are the objectives, don't do the other things. They wanted to take the towns which were not ours. Those were the objectives and not this other thing. Republika Srpska, it needs to be divided, the corridor, these were all the objectives that we had a right to, so I don't see why I wouldn't say that at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning quickly to 65 ter 06305, English pages 37 through 41 and B/C/S 33 through 37. This is an extract of the war diary from General Simic from August 1992 to December 1995. And his entry for the same date. If we could continue through the document. Next page, please. Sorry, if we could see the -- I know it's difficult to show both, but the entirety of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see reflections of the same information reflected in General Mladic's diary. Your expression of concern about criticism of the SDS and your defence of the SDS, and then your annunciation of the strategic goals. So at this meeting with the military on September 2nd, Mr. Krajisnik, it's clear that, once again, the Bosnian Serb leadership, this time through you, reminded the military of the goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really trying to understand your question. The strategic objectives were used a hundred times during the war because that was a public document, our political platform for negotiations with foreigners. And on this occasion I know precisely there was a heated discussion between the civilians, the civilian leadership, so to speak, and the army, where they criticised the Serbian Democratic Party and local municipal authorities and they had a hundred objectives and complaints against the civilians. And they requested that some -- their plans about the division of Bosnia down the valley of Usora River should be applied, like half of Bosnia would be Serbian and half Croatian, and Tuzla should belong to Serbs. And then we said: Look, wait, the strategic objectives that we have are that all three sides have the right to this Bosnia. Bosnia is not only Serbian. And the army wanted -- it says here the alliance of communist movement for Yugoslavia. These were the communists who idealised the situation and wanted to establish a new Yugoslavia which was completely unrealistic. So whatever I said was I recall their megalomaniac objectives so this would be put into perspective and that they would pursue the policy, which they didn't want to. Instead they were criticising the policy and believed that the army should resolve everything in the way that it saw fit. That was the objective, rather than the objective was: Gentlemen, here are the war objectives, go into the war and take the Muslim territories. Each strategic objective was our right. To what in accordance to the agreement with Cutileiro and everybody else, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you don't need to explain each time. I want to turn to a meeting of November 8th, this is yet another meeting that took place before the issuance of directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's found at P1481 beginning at page 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you minded to tender that portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object to pages 37 through 40 which is that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did General Simic testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, he died. We would have liked to apply 92 quater but we didn't ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a meeting of the 8th of November with the corps commanders, and as we can see, the various corps commanders submitted their reports first. So it's a very exacting military briefing. First General Talic, the commander of the 1 KK; then Colonel Boric, the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps; Colonel Lisica, commander of the Doboj Operations Group; Colonel Simic, commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps; Colonel Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps, and so on. And at page 145, Dr. Karadzic states that: "The army and our courageous officers contributed enormously to the results that we have achieved to date." We notice -- next page, he notes at page 146 that there is some political concern about operations. The West finds the fall of towns frightening, but then notes: "Maybe it would be good if we solved: "The issue of the Drina." And then you speak, Mr. Krajisnik, and you say: "I admire the military successes. "It is very dangerous to seize their territories. "The Drina and the Neretva ..." And then you state that: "We," meaning the Bosnian Serbs, the political and military authorities, "have a disproportionate engagement of the army in relation to the strategic objectives." And as it notes in the other page, you state: "We have not achieved: "The Neretva, the sea, and the Podrinje area." But note that: "We have achieved: "The corridor and separation with the Muslims." And you continue that: "The most pressing thing is to mop up Orasje and then to solve the problem of the Podrinje area and the Neretva River Valley as soon as possible. "The Muslims must not stay with us and they should not be given any kind of autonomy. "The most important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic - the ciscenje of the Drina. "The most important task is separation from the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just go back to the page before that, the previous page, and then could we go back to this one. Please, just the Serbian version. This is a confirmation of what I said a moment ago. "It is very dangerous to take their territories." And then I said the Drina and the Neretva, it's probably our strategic objective. I'm saying that: "We have this disproportionate engagement of the army in relation to the strategic objectives." Can we now go back to the previous page, or rather, the next page. Here also: "Separation with the Muslims," all right. "The most important objective is," I saw that somewhere, is to end the war as far as I can remember. It says so somewhere. Ah, yes, "we must bring the war to an end." That is probably what the situation was. It is not written there. Soldiers presented different proposals and I mentioned some; that is to say, Tuzla should be in Republika Srpska. You saw a moment ago Gradacac, Bugojno, and so on. I said there: Gentlemen, there are political objectives. You cannot take something that is our policy and ours. The war should be brought to an end as soon as possible. It was not my opinion; it was the opinion of the political leadership. And what is mentioned here, separation, all the time, separation is the establishment of our own constituent unit. And our objective was the following: If we could not remain in Yugoslavia, if somebody kicked us out, then we reached this compromise with the international community. You will get your constituent unit within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And national homogenisation should be applied or, rather, the ethnic key to establish your constituent unit. So that is the basic objective, a replacement for Yugoslavia. We lost our state and got our constituent unit. That's what I'm highlighting here. I don't know how he interpreted this and how he refers to it, but I recognise that those are exactly the traces, or rather, the paths as set by the political leadership in the war, to reach peace as soon as possible even by conceding territory, but not by taking the territory of others. The large territory that was liberated by our army, and that is 5 or 6 per cent more than we had, according to the land register, that created problems during the negotiations. That's a problem when you have too much territory, you cannot chart a proper map, you cannot reach agreement, and you don't know which territory should be returned. Everybody at local level wants to have other territories returned, not theirs, so that was a disadvantage for us rather than an advantage. Of course it's not an advantage to have a very small territory like at the very end, but 70 per cent of the territory was a problem for us. It had to be reduced to 49 per cent and that is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so in order to reduce the territory, according to you, you said: Here's what we've achieved so far, the corridor, that was achieved by the military, right, Operation Corridor? That was a military achievement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that we had agreed with the Croats on how this could be resolved politically. Of course, when it is not possible to resolve it politically and people were dying there because there was a humanitarian disaster, then the military made a corridor there, very small, 3 kilometres, no more, so that a truck could pass through. Didn't take Orasje, didn't take Gradacac, didn't take a larger territory, although they did leave part of Serb territory on their side. So this was a humanitarian necessity, the army had to take that. There didn't have to be a task involved. If 12 babies died at a maternity ward, of course people felt: Yes, we should all break through this corridor so that we could have humanitarian aid provided. Also, the Neretva, we did not manage to achieve that. Our army was on the Neretva river when the JNA was there, when they were leaving. But, quite simply, they withdrew from an area that was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Three of the strategic objectives that hadn't been achieved by that date were the Neretva, access to the sea, and the Podrinje area. You pointed out the disproportionate allocation of military resources to the overall strategic objectives and said: Right now the most important task -- the most important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic, the commander of the Drina Corps, and that is the "ciscenje" of the Drina, and that objective was reflected in directive 4 which was issued on November 19th. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My participation in the discussion had nothing to do with the directive. I did not know what kind of directive had been made and I did not quote these directives. I just said at that meeting -- I remember that meeting very well. The situation was tense at that meeting between the civilian and the military representatives. They had different ideas of their own as to what should be done. I was just trying to channel things and to say what our political objective was, and the objective was not to cleanse the Drina. Of course, there were a lot of hostilities there and a lot of blood was shed on both sides. So I was just saying what the strategic was and that was the corridor. You saw our map, corridor, contiguous territory, and the enclaves should remain in the eastern part of Republika Srpska, of course, in the western part, Serb ethnic territory should remain. So we did lose that afterwards, so we ultimately, in the final solution, got things that did not involve a majority Serb population and we lost others that -- where Serbs were not the majority population, but that was not our objective throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These last lines, it seems that we lost what was ours and we got what was ours. The witness said that we lost something that had been purely Serb and we got something where the Serbs were not a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue tomorrow, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.00 p.m.,
